items.title: Mapping vocational e-learning research: A bibliometric analysis
items.abstract: Vocational e-learning has become increasingly important as vocational education systems respond to digital transformation, changing labour-market demands, and the need for flexible skills development. However, research on vocational e-learning remains scattered across educational technology, vocational education, vocational training, workforce development, and professional skills development. This study maps the evolution, knowledge architecture, and thematic structure of vocational e-learning research through a bibliometric analysis of publications indexed in the Web of Science. A topic search was conducted on April 28, 2026, without setting a publication year limit. After restricting the results to English-language journal articles, 1,014 records were retained for analysis. Publication trend analysis, citation analysis, country-level co-authorship analysis, co-citation analysis, and author keyword co-occurrence analysis were conducted using VOSviewer. The findings show that vocational e-learning research gradually expanded after 2006 and accelerated after 2019, reaching a publication peak in 2022. The United States, England, and the People’s Republic of China were among the main contributors, although national-level collaboration remained uneven. Co-citation analysis revealed five intellectual clusters related to online and blended learning foundations, emergency online learning, vocational and simulation-based training, technology acceptance, and digital pedagogy or technology-enhanced learning. Author keyword co-occurrence analysis identified several thematic clusters, including blended learning, vocational education, e-learning, work-based learning, simulation, immersive technologies, and digital transformation. Overall, the study maps vocational e-learning as a boundary-spanning field shaped by general online learning, vocational and clinical training, technology acceptance, digital pedagogy, and practice-oriented learning. It suggests that future research should move beyond online content delivery toward authentic skill development, learner engagement, competency assessment, workplace learning, employability, and technology-enhanced vocational pedagogy.

items.title: Musculoskeletal Pain and Postural Abnormalities among Lebanese University Students: Prevalence and Correlates from a Cross-Sectional Study
items.abstract: Abstract Background Musculoskeletal (MSK) pain is a major global health concern and is increasingly recognized among university students due to prolonged sedentary behavior, extensive digital device use, and academic demands. In Lebanon, data on MSK pain within this population remain limited. This study aims to determine the prevalence of MSK pain and postural abnormalities among Lebanese university students and to identify demographic, academic, lifestyle, and health-related factors associated with MSK pain. Methods A cross-sectional study using the Extended Nordic Musculoskeletal Questionnaire (NMQ-E) and the Internet Addiction Test (IAT) was conducted among 396 university students from higher education institutions across Lebanon. Participants completed a structured questionnaire incorporating these validated instruments, along with questions on sociodemographic characteristics, academic behaviors, ergonomic practices, lifestyle factors, and medical conditions. Descriptive statistics, bivariate analyses, multivariable logistic regression, and multiple linear regression were performed. Results The findings indicate a high lifetime prevalence of MSK pain, particularly in the neck (68.7%), lower back (69.2%), and shoulders (60.9%). In multivariable analysis, female sex is independently associated with higher odds of MSK pain across multiple regions (aOR = 1.9–2.8, 95% CI: 1.0–5.3, p < 0.05). Self-perceived poor posture shows a strong association with lower back pain (aOR = 2.0, 95% CI: 1.01–4.14, p < 0.05), upper back pain, wrist/hand pain, and overall pain burden. Sleep disorders (aOR = 2.3–3.0, 95% CI: 1.03–7.02, p < 0.05) and migraine (aOR = 2.3, 95% CI: 1.26–4.05, p < 0.01) are also independently associated with increased MSK pain. In linear regression, male sex is associated with a lower overall pain score (β = −0.16, p < 0.01), while poor posture and comorbid conditions remain significant predictors of higher pain scores. Conclusion MSK pain is highly prevalent among Lebanese university students and is influenced by a combination of ergonomic, academic, lifestyle, and health-related factors. These findings highlight the importance of implementing university-based prevention strategies that promote ergonomic awareness, healthy study behaviors, and student well-being to reduce the burden of MSK pain.

items.title: Neural Representations as New Modes of Interactivity
items.abstract: Human-AI interaction today runs almost entirely through prompts and outputs, keeping AI systems opaque to general users. We introduce Neural Representation Interaction (NRI), a paradigm that treats the internal representations of neural networks as an interaction material people can inspect, steer, and edit. Situating NRI alongside graphical, tangible, and bio-computer interaction, we argue that the concepts and algorithms models encode internally offer representational affordances for richer human-AI interaction. We synthesize actionable mechanistic interpretability methods and, drawing on General Morphological Analysis, construct a design space spanning Interaction, Target, Referent, and Purpose. Mapping existing interfaces onto this space reveals that most serve expert auditors, while few support lay users. We then present speculative applications in education, personal user modeling, and hiring audits, and discuss design principles, limitations, and sociotechnical risks. NRI offers HCI researchers abstractions for designing interactions that work with AI computation rather than only through its inputs and outputs.

items.title: Occupational Safety Knowledge and Personal Protective Equipment Practices among Retail Butchers in the Cauvery Delta Region of Tamil Nadu, India
items.abstract: Retail butchers encounter occupational hazards associated with sharp instruments and meat handling. This cross-sectional survey assessed occupational health and safety knowledge, personal protective equipment (PPE) knowledge and reported use, and injury-prevention awareness among 200 retail butchers in the Cauvery Delta region of Tamil Nadu, India, during May–June 2026. The study covered Thanjavur, Tiruvarur, Nagapattinam and Mayiladuthurai districts and used a structured questionnaire containing 29 occupational health and safety items. Knowledge scores were classified as poor (0–14), moderate (15–21) or good (22–29). Of the respondents, 72 (36.0%) reported previous formal occupational-safety training and 128 (64.0%) reported none. Knowledge of the protective roles of aprons and gloves was reported by 75.0% and 73.0%, respectively, whereas reported use was 61.0% and 42.0%, respectively. These figures derive from separate knowledge and use items and do not establish individual-level compliance. Safe knife handling, immediate first aid and prompt injury reporting were recognised by 79.0%, 77.0% and 64.0% of respondents, respectively. Overall, 32.0% had good knowledge, 41.0% moderate knowledge and 27.0% poor knowledge. Good knowledge was recorded for 43.1% of trained respondents and 25.8% of untrained respondents. Knowledge category was associated with previous training (Pearson’s χ²(2, N = 200) = 8.76, p = 0.013). The findings identify differences between aggregate knowledge and self-reported use measures and an association between previous training and knowledge, without demonstrating causality.

items.title: Off- Campus Learning Experience and Personality Development of Swimming Team: Inputs for Policy Insights
items.abstract: Abstract. This study examined the off-campus learning experiences and personal development of swimming team members under curriculum innovation initiatives in the Division of Agusan del Sur to inform policy insights. It assessed off-campus learning experiences in terms of skill development, sportsmanship and teamwork, discipline and time management, motivation and self-confidence, and academic responsibility; determined the extent of development across emotional, behavioral, cognitive, and social dimensions; and examined the relationships among these variables. A descriptive-correlational research design was employed. The participants were 34 Grade 6 swimming team members selected through total enumeration. Data were gathered using a structured questionnaire and analyzed through frequency and percentage, weighted mean, and Spearman rank-order correlation. Results showed effective off-campus learning experiences. Motivation and self-confidence obtained the highest mean (4.50), followed by sportsmanship and teamwork (4.49), discipline and time management (4.36), academic responsibility (4.31), and skill development (4.05). Among the measured dimensions, cognitive engagement obtained the highest mean (4.15), followed by behavioral (4.14), emotional (4.04), and social development (approximately 4.02). Most relationships between off-campus learning experiences and developmental dimensions were not statistically significant. Sportsmanship and teamwork showed inverse associations with behavioral engagement (ρ = −.355, p = .040) and social engagement (ρ = −.397, p = .020) at the unadjusted level. However, neither association remained statistically significant after adjustment for multiple comparisons. The study proposed an Enhanced Off-Campus Learning Experience and Learner Development Policy to strengthen structured learning, holistic development, academic coordination, safety, inclusion, and regular monitoring. items.title: Perceived workload and associated organizational factors among healthcare professionals in emergency departments of referral hospitals in Conakry, Guinea: a multicenter cross-sectional study
items.abstract: Abstract Background Workload affects occupational health, staff well-being and quality of care. Emergency departments are particularly demanding, especially in resource-limited settings. This study assessed perceived workload and associated organizational and professional factors among healthcare professionals working in referral hospital emergency departments in Conakry, Guinea. Methods We conducted a multicenter analytical cross-sectional study from March 2 to June 2, 2026, in the emergency departments of Donka University Hospital, Ignace Deen University Hospital and the Sino-Guinean Hospital. Eligible physicians and nurses were exhaustively recruited. Perceived workload was measured using the NASA Task Load Index, and associated factors were examined using bivariate analyses and multiple linear regression. Results A total of 146 healthcare professionals were included; the median age was 32 years, and nurses represented 58.9% of participants. The median weekly working time was 56 hours. The overall NASA-TLX score indicated a high perceived workload, mainly driven by mental demand, physical demand and overall effort. In multivariable analysis, being aged 30–39 years was associated with a higher workload score, whereas perceived adequate staffing was associated with a lower score. A moderate work atmosphere was also associated with increased workload compared with a good work atmosphere. Conclusions Perceived workload among emergency department healthcare professionals in Conakry was high and was mainly associated with organizational determinants, particularly staffing adequacy and work atmosphere. Interventions should strengthen human resources, improve the work environment and help prevent psychosocial risks. Trial registration: Not applicable. This study was an observational cross-sectional survey and did not evaluate a health care intervention on human participants.

items.title: Pilot Study on Scale Reliability and Model Validity for Human and Technological Factors Influencing Smart Transportation Service Performance
items.abstract: This pilot study is to test the reliability of measurement scales and the validity of the research model used to study human and technological factors that impact smart transportation service performance. A quantitative method was used in which a structured questionnaire was used to gather data from a population of 30 participants relevant to the smart transportation context in Amman, Jordan. The study aims to evaluate the internal consistency of the measurement items in each of the three internal dimensions of the study, of which the three dimensions of the human factor (Smart Transportation Awareness, Perceived Safety, Social Influence) and three dimensions of the technological factor (Performance Expectancy, Effort Expectancy, Facilitating Condition, System Integration, and Data Privacy) are examined, and to confirm the correctness of the relations of constructs in the model, namely Smart Transportation Service Performance. The findings show satisfactory reliability of all the measurement scales and acceptable validity of the model, which allows us to use the model in further large-scale empirical studies. The result of this pilot study is considered to be a methodological foundation for further research and the strength of the developed research instrument for the study of the performance of smart transportation services.

items.title: Point-of-Care Electroanalytical Technologies for Lithium Carbonate Monitoring in Bipolar Affective Disorders
items.abstract: Abstract Lithium (Li), administered as lithium salts such as lithium carbonate (Li2CO3), remains a gold-standard maintenance treatment for bipolar affective disorder (bipolar disorder), but its narrow therapeutic index requires regular monitoring of lithium−ion (Li+) concentrations. This review critically examines electroanalytical strategies for decentralized Li measurement, including conventional electrodes, screen-printed electrodes, wearable platforms, and minimally invasive sampling. Attention is given to ion-selective recognition, manganese (Mn)-spinel intercalation materials, matrix effects, and the evidence supporting saliva, sweat, interstitial fluid, and capillary blood. The available literature supports these matrices as promising adjuncts but not as universal replacements for standardized venous testing. Their clinical use still requires paired matrix validation, control of sampling time and environmental effects, long-term sensor stability studies, and explicit confirmatory testing rules for suspected toxicity. Laser-induced graphene and fused deposition modeling are therefore discussed only as enabling fabrication concepts rather than as established Li-sensing technologies. Finally, the review outlines regulatory, human factor, connectivity, and healthcare integration requirements that must be addressed before wearable or home-use Li devices can support routine care.

items.title: Promotion focus, growth i-deals and service creativity: a regulatory focus perspective
items.abstract: Purpose Given that content- and timing-based idiosyncratic deals (i-deals) are inherently heterogeneous across employees and contexts, this study shifts attention to motivation-oriented growth i-deals. Drawing on regulatory focus theory (RFT) and the ability–motivation–opportunity (AMO) model, the study seeks to examine the antecedents, outcomes, chain mediating paths and boundary conditions of growth i-deals. Design/methodology/approach Multiwave, multisource and multilevel data were collected from 600 frontline employees in 100 hotel and mall teams in China. A cross-level moderated mediation model was tested using multilevel path analysis in Mplus and 20,000 Monte Carlo simulations. Findings Four key findings have been obtained. First, promotion focus is positively associated with growth i-deals. Second, growth i-deals positively predict three AMO variables (creative self-efficacy, intrinsic motivation and perceived participation opportunity) that further promote service creativity. Third, team-level servant leadership moderates the main effect of promotion focus on growth i-deals. Finally, team-level servant leadership moderates the indirect effects of promotion focus on service creativity via the chain mediation path of growth i-deals and three AMO variables. The main effect and the indirect effects are stronger when team-level servant leadership is high rather than low. Practical implications Hotel firms should attend to employees’ underlying developmental motives and effectively channel their developmental aspirations through i-deals. Furthermore, hotel firms should place greater emphasis on cultivating servant leaders by encouraging managers to exhibit servant leadership behaviors and providing leadership training. Originality/value This study broadens the scope of i-deals research from traditional focus on i-deals content and timing to the focus on i-deals motivation. Moreover, the study extends RFT and AMO model by investigating the antecedent, outcome, mechanisms and contingencies of growth i-deals, particularly in hospitality and related service settings.

items.title: Reduced-Port Robotic Living Donor Nephrectomy Using the da Vinci Xi Platform: A Comparative Cohort Study of SP+1 RDN, Multi-port Robotic, and Laparoendoscopic Single-Site Techniques
items.abstract: Abstract Background Living donor nephrectomy is performed in healthy individuals and therefore demands a particularly high safety threshold. Robotic donor nephrectomy may improve visualization, dexterity, and ergonomics, while reduced-port approaches seek to decrease abdominal wall trauma. Dedicated da Vinci SP platforms enable true single-port robotic surgery but are not universally available. We evaluated a single-port-plus-one (SP + 1 RDN) configuration performed with the conventional da Vinci Xi platform and compared it with laparoendoscopic single-site donor nephrectomy (LESS-DN) and conventional multi-port robotic donor nephrectomy (RDN). Methods This retrospective single-centre cohort included 808 living kidney donors in a prospectively maintained institutional database. Only 3 surgical techniques were included: 59 Xi SP + 1 RDN, 706 LESS-DN, and 43 multi-port RDN. Continuous variables were compared by one-way analysis of variance, with Tukey-adjusted post-hoc comparisons where appropriate; categorical variables were compared using chi-square testing. The Xi SP + 1 RDN technique used a 4–5 cm periumbilical GelPort containing the camera/working access and a 12-mm AirSeal assistant port, plus one upper quadrant 8-mm robotic port. Results Mean age was 36.5 ± 9.6 years in SP + 1 RDN, 33.4 ± 8.1 years in LESS-DN, and 34.7 ± 8.9 years in Multi-port RDN (P=.012). BMI was similar among groups (P=.378). Mean warm ischaemia time was 4.36 ± 1.24, 3.53 ± 1.02, and 4.05 ± 1.08 minutes, respectively (P<.001). Mean operative time was 178.1 ± 28.5 minutes for SP + 1 RDN, 193.0 ± 51.8 minutes for LESS-DN, and 254.8 ± 45.5 minutes for Multi-port RDN (P<.001). Median length of stay was 2 days in all groups. All 59 SP + 1 RDN procedures were completed robotically without transfusion or conversion; one intraoperative bleeding episode was controlled robotically. Conclusions Reduced-port SP + 1 RDN donor nephrectomy using the da Vinci Xi platform is feasible and preserves short warm ischaemia time and a reasonably short operative time compared with the centre’s earlier multi-port robotic experience. The approach should be regarded as an Xi-based reduced-port configuration—not as da Vinci SP surgery. Its principal practical advantage is the ability to pursue port reduction while retaining triangulation, assistant access, and existing Xi infrastructure.

items.title: Score 2 Cardiovascular Risk Assessment in Healthcare and Public Service Workers in Northeastern Italy
items.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To evaluate cardiovascular (CV) risk across occupational groups using SCORE2 in healthy workers undergoing occupational surveillance. METHODS: A cross-sectional study included 5,956 workers aged ≥40 years undergoing occupational examinations in Northeast Italy (2023-2025). CV risk was estimated using SCORE2. Associations with demographic, lifestyle, and occupational variables were assessed using nonparametric tests and multivariable regression. RESULTS: Most workers had low CV risk (83.3%). Higher SCORE2 was associated with smoking (β = 1.40, 95% CI 1.07-1.74), higher BMI (β = 0.11 per kg/m², p<0.001), and occupational role. Technical/logistics staff and municipal police officers had the highest estimates, whereas administrative and healthcare workers had lower scores. Night-shift work was not associated with CV risk (β = -0.07, 95% CI -0.17; 0.04). CONCLUSIONS: SCORE2 may support CV risk stratification and targeted prevention in occupational health.

items.title: Serum Creatinine Levels among Motorcycle Workshop Mechanics in Carbon Monoxide-Prone Workplaces: A Photometric Study
items.abstract: Motorcycle workshop mechanics work in environments where vehicle exhaust may accumulate, particularly in workshops located near dense traffic and with limited ventilation. Carbon monoxide (CO) is not directly measured in this study; therefore, daily working hours and years of employment are used as occupational indicators of possible long-term exposure. This descriptive cross-sectional study analyzed serum creatinine levels among 30 motorcycle workshop mechanics on Jalan Riau, Pekanbaru. Respondents were selected by purposive sampling based on predefined eligibility criteria. Venous blood was collected, processed into serum, and analyzed using an Optiva photometer with a Glory Diagnostics enzymatic creatinine kit at 510 nm. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize creatinine distribution by age, daily working duration, and length of employment. The results showed that 17 respondents (56.67%) had serum creatinine levels above the reference range (>1.3 mg/dL), while 13 respondents (43.33%) had normal levels (0.7-1.3 mg/dL). Increased creatinine levels were more frequent among mechanics working 12 hours/day (75%) than among those working 8 hours/day (20%), and were also more common in respondents aged 30 years or older and those with more than 10 years of employment. These findings suggest that mechanics with longer occupational contact in CO-prone workshop environments may have a higher proportion of elevated serum creatinine. However, because ambient CO or carboxyhemoglobin was not measured, the results should be interpreted as an occupational-health screening finding rather than evidence of direct causality. Improved ventilation, routine health monitoring, and occupational safety education are recommended.

items.title: Smart Underwear System Based on Real-Time Strain Gauge Measurement of Nocturnal Penile Tumescence (NPT) and Optimal Coital Timing Prediction Algorithm: Monetizing the 'Morning Glory'
items.abstract: Healthy adult males experience nocturnal penile tumescence (NPT) 3 to 5 times per night during rapid eye movement (REM) sleep. Throughout human history, this substantial biomechanical energy has remained entirely unmonetized and squandered in unconsciousness. Building upon the pioneering textile-urological investigations of Shafik (2007 Ig Nobel Prize in Medicine), this study introduces the design and N=1 proof-of-concept evaluation of 'Smart Briefs v1.0'—an ergonomic wearable system integrating carbon nanotube (CNT) stretchable conductive fabric, a polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) piezoelectric tenting-pressure sensor, and a negative temperature coefficient (NTC) scrotal thermistor. Real-time circumferential strain, axial rigidity, and duration are transmitted via Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) to a smartphone application. We formulate the Golden-Time Index (GTI) algorithm, which filters out bladder-filling reflex tumescence (Morning-After-Pee Syndrome, MAPS) and sleep-posture artifacts to identify optimal physiological windows for coitus. A 28-night single-subject self-experimentation protocol demonstrated a 97.9% reduction in prone-position false alarms ("The 03:00 AM Crisis") via 3-axis gyroscope posture compensation. By converting unconscious nocturnal physiological events into actionable push notifications and meteorological intimacy forecasts, this research advances domestic reproductive timing from intuitive guesswork to precision data science.

items.title: Social, but not that social: No evidence that robots trigger self-categorization
items.abstract: This paper investigates through two experiments whether robots form a social category strong enough to trigger self-categorization in participants. Self-categorization theory poses that salient social groups influence people's self-concept, so that activation of an in-group category may cause people to define themselves more in line with the group stereotype, while activation of an out-group triggers a contrasting response. Social categorization thus exerts a subtle but pervasive influence as self-concept affects attitudes, cognition, and behavior. Previous research has shown that humans apply human social categories (such as race and gender) to robots. This research tests whether robots form their own social category strong enough to cause a temporary shift in humans’ active self-concept. In two online experiments participants were primed with humans, robots, or no social category. Self-categorization was recorded by both spontaneous and prompted self-report: participants completed a freehand self-description (which was coded for the extent to which it contained traits that set humans apart from robots) and rated themselves on a set of both desirable and undesirable human-specific traits. MANOVA was used to test the overall effect of condition, ANOVAs to follow up on individual measures. The first experiment ( N = 123) gave ambiguous results, as MANOVA indicated significant differences in self-categorization between the three conditions, but no differences were found for any of the individual DVs. To better interpret these results, a the second experiment provided a conceptual replication with a stronger experimental manipulation and larger sample ( N = 233). No significant differences between the three conditions were found for any of the self-categorization measures. Equivalence between conditions was established on the explicitly prompted measures, further supporting interpretations that priming did not yield any effect. This suggests that while robots may adopt human social categories, they currently do not form a social category of their own that triggers self-categorization processes.

items.title: Stress Levels and Teaching Performance of Secondary English Teachers in Bantayan, Cebu Province
items.abstract: This study examined occupational stress and teaching performance among 100 secondary English teachers from 14 schools on Bantayan Island, Cebu Province, during the 2024-2025 academic year. A descriptive-comparative and correlational research design was employed. Data were collected using a perceived work stress questionnaire and existing Classroom Observation Tool ratings. The findings indicated a moderate overall stress level, with work overload and role ambiguity emerging as prominent workplace concerns. Teachers demonstrated high intrinsic motivation, moderate extrinsic motivation, and generally very satisfactory to outstanding teaching performance. Most demographic and professional characteristics showed no statistically significant differences in stress levels. However, the reported analysis indicated a significant difference by sex. The relationship between occupational stress and teaching performance was weak and statistically non-significant. The findings highlight the importance of manageable workloads, clearly defined responsibilities, professional development, and institutional support in promoting teacher well-being. Further research involving broader populations and additional organizational factors is recommended.

items.title: Swedish teachers’ perceived professional action competence in sustainability and climate change education
items.abstract: This study aims to explore how in-service school teachers in Sweden perceive their professional action competence (PAC) in Sustainability and Climate Change Education (SCCE). Drawing on data from an exploratory survey involving 202 primary and secondary school teachers in Sweden, the study examines three core dimensions of PAC in SCCE: professional knowledge, self-efficacy, and willingness to teach. Descriptive and frequency analyses were employed to identify teachers’ self-perceptions across these dimensions. The study reveals that teachers generally perceive their professional action competence in SCCE as well-prepared, particularly regarding content knowledge and teaching approaches, and they report high levels of intrinsic motivation for teaching SCCE. However, the results also show several areas across these dimensions in which teachers felt less prepared: (1) to facilitate collective action-taking by students, (2) to engage with community partners beyond school in the teaching and learning process, (3) to support students in dealing with difficult emotions, and (4) to assess students’ sustainability-related competences. The study provides valuable insights into the conditions that support or constrain the implementation of SCCE in schools and aims to inform the design of future professional development initiatives and contribute to ongoing efforts to strengthen teachers’ preparedness for transformative SCCE.

items.title: TDDM-Melatt: A Decoupled Memory and Diffusion Framework for Generalizable Encrypted Traffic Classification
items.abstract: The widespread adoption of encrypted traffic poses severe challenges to current security situational awareness systems based on network traffic monitoring. In existing dataset-driven training and testing studies, limitations such as shortcut learning induced by spurious feature correlations and sample imbalance caused by the long-tail distribution of real-world traffic result in weak generalization of traffic identification performance to real-world network traffic. To address these limitations, we propose TDDM-Melatt. First, we design Melatt, a memory-decoupled traffic representation model, which employs Competitive Gating Long Short-Term Memory (CG-LSTM) to construct the encoder and decoder. We design a spurious-correlation-free pre-training and inference paradigm, employing strict topology anonymization and a frozen pre-trained encoder strategy to cut off the model's learning pathways for spurious features. Second, we propose a Traffic Denoising Diffusion Model (TDDM) tailored to the characteristics of traffic data. Addressing the structured nature of high-dimensional sparsity and strong feature correlations in traffic data, we solve the problem of having only class labels as conditional guidance for traffic diffusion models. Extensive experiments are conducted on 4 representative public benchmark datasets. Under strict flow-level splitting and anonymization, TDDM-Melatt outperforms 6 basic classification models and 6 SOTA representation learning models. The proposed method provides a new and effective technical pathway for encrypted traffic classification in real-world network environments.

items.title: Teams Perform Better When They Make Progress Together Through Talk
items.abstract: Effective team communication depends not only on what is said but also on whether each exchange advances task execution. This study developed an utterance-level progress metric to characterize communication as forward, backward, sideways, or pause and examined its relationship with team performance. Forty-eight participants completed a cooperative, time-constrained defusal task, yielding 95 cases. Speech acts and progress were coded from transcripts with strong interrater reliability for speech acts (κ = 0.83) and moderate reliability for progress (κ = 0.60). Good-performance cases showed more forward progress and less backward and sideways progress than poor-performance cases. Poor performance was also associated with a higher prevalence of information requests, while pause utterances were longer during good performance. Adding progress variables significantly improved a speech-act-only classification model, although cross-validated improvement was inconclusive. These findings suggest that speech acts and utterance-by-utterance progress provide complementary indicators of team coordination and performance.

items.title: Technologies for Visualizing Organizational and Educational Information from the Standpoint of Pedagogical Neurodesign
items.abstract: Purpose of the study. The paper provides a theoretical justification and a practical test of technologies for visualizing organizational and educational information that are constructed from the standpoint of pedagogical neurodesign and the services, implemented with generative neural network available to users in Russia. The relevance of the paper follows from the expanding capabilities of artificial intelligence in the preparation of visual materials. Visualization facilitates the perception of educational and organizational material and contributes to the strength of its assimilation; however, visualization remains a labor-intensive process requiring special training form the lecturer in the graphical presentation of information. Generative neural network services reduce this labour intensity and make the preparation of an image available to the teacher without a designer, so the central question becomes what the technologies of visualization should be like for the result to match the didactic task, the regularities of visual perception and the limits of the learner’s working memory. The objectives are to clarify the notion of pedagogical neurodesign and to highlight the parameters of the visual presentation of information, to compare the output formats of visual objects and create a model for choosing a format, as well as to describe the software that reproduces this model. Materials and methods. The theoretical basis includes cognitive load theory, the cognitive theory of multimedia learning, dual coding theory, ergonomic requirements for visual presentation of information, the work of domestic researchers on visualization of educational information and on the use of artificial intelligence in vocational education. The methods applied are theoretical analysis and generalization, a comparative analysis of generative neural network services as of July 2026, pedagogical design and prototyping of the software. The empirical basis is the experience of the Laboratory of pedagogical design and virtual reality of the technopark of universal pedagogical competencies named after M.I. Shilova at Krasnoyarsk State Pedagogical University named after V.P. Astafyev. Results. The subjects of visualization of educational and organizational information are identified, which are presented to the learner together and differ in the didactic purpose of the image. The notion of pedagogical neurodesign is clarified, correlated with the smart approach and separated from the instrumental layer of generative services. Six parameters of visual presentation are identified, namely coloristics, typography, contrast, symmetry and unity of form, free space and pictography, for each of which psychophysiological foundation, a design requirement and the consequence of non- compliance are indicated. Five output formats of visual objects are compared and the conditions of their application are defined. A model of format selection is constructed that comprises five steps, from the identification of the type of information to the verification of the result against five criteria. The smart visualization wizard is described, located in the public domain and implementing the specified model in the form of a step-by-step web application. Examples of the visualization of organizational and educational information obtained using it are presented. Conclusion. items.title: The Catalyst UX Framework: Sustained User Research with Empirical Insights for Complex GIS Systems
items.abstract: This paper presents the Catalyst UX framework, a five-stage participatory design process developed to support the creation of highly technical Geographic Information System (GIS) platforms. GIS user experience can suffer from steep learning curves, fragmented workflows, and declining engagement once development shifts toward technical implementation. Catalyst UX addresses this challenge through sustained engagement with domain experts across workshops, a Technical Working Group (TWG), individual interviews, usability testing, and product launch activities. The framework was implemented during the development of a water data observatory integrating 21 datasets for hydrology and water resource management. This paper discusses qualitative and quantitative findings from a mixed-methods usability study ( n = 12) demonstrating a 93% task completion rate and a System Usability Scale (SUS) score of 60 for the minimum viable product. Results suggest that continuous expert engagement improved feature prioritization, reduced scope creep, and preserved alignment between system architecture and analytical workflows in GIS environments.

items.title: The face matching performance of human-algorithm teams over time (EFCT)
items.abstract: We often need to identify someone based on their facial appearance. In applied settings, verification is commonly a one-to-one matching task, in which we compare an individual’s appearance to the photograph on their identification document (such as a driver’s licence or passport). While face matching was once only performed by humans, it is becoming more common for the task to incorporate facial recognition technologies, such as Automated Facial Recognition (AFR) systems. While specific details about how the human and technology operate together are often situationally dependent, here we are interested in a general paradigm in which the algorithm provides the human with a prediction to evaluate (i.e., whether the two images show the “same” person or two “different” people), but the human has full control over the final identification decision made. Unaided by technology, human performance on unfamiliar face matching tasks is often characterised as being “error prone”, with average accuracy of 60-90% common in standardised laboratory tasks (for a review see Fysh & Bindemann, 2017). On high quality imagery, modern facial recognition systems that leverage Deep Convolutional Neural Networks can achieve exceptional levels of accuracy that exceed human performance (Carragher & Hancock, 2020; Grother et al., 2025; White et al., 2015). But our past research has shown that while humans can improve their own face matching performance when using algorithms as decision aids, the average aided performance of the human is significantly worse than the algorithm alone (Carragher & Hancock, 2023). That is, the average human fails to correct algorithm errors, while also overturning correct decisions from the system (see also Carragher et al., 2024; Hua et al., 2025). In our research so far, participants have been novices (either undergraduate students or members of the public), who have completed a laboratory face matching task with assistance from a simulated Automated Facial Recognition (sAFR) system. In Carragher and Hancock (2023), participants completed the Expertise in Facial Comparison Task (EFCT: White et al., 2015), which consists of 168 trials in total. However, with the procedure we had at the time, participants only completed half the trials (84) with assistance from the algorithm. In Carragher et al. (2024), participants completed the short version of the Glasgow Face Matching Test 2 (GFMT2-S: White et al., 2022), which consists of 80 trials total, but again only had assistance from the algorithm on half the trials. In Hua et al. (2025), participants completed 78 trials with algorithm assistance, in a task that combined the short Kent Face Matching Task (KFMT: Fysh & Bindemann, 2018a) and the unfamiliar portion of the Stirling Familiar Face Matching Task (Carragher & Hancock, 2020). In Mueller et al. (2024), participants completed 160 trials with assistance from an algorithm. The longest algorithm assisted face matching task we are aware of was conducted by Fysh and Bindemann (2018b), who had participants complete 210 trials from the Kent University Face Database (Fysh & Bindemann, 2018a) – however, the algorithm in this study was relatively inaccurate, providing the correct response on 60% of trials (for further discussion see Carragher and Hancock, 2023). The face matching tasks in these experiments would all take less than 30 minutes to complete (some of these papers do not report experiment duration, but on average, participants submit face matching decisions in about 5 seconds – see Fysh & Bindemann, 2018a). Human-algorithm teaming for face matching is likely to occur in applied settings where operators are professional staff. In these settings, it is possible that a shift may last longer than 30 minutes. Studies of human face matching ability suggest that performance decreases as the task progresses. Alenezi and Bindemann (2015) had participants complete the same 200 trial face matching task 5 times in a single session, for 1000 trials total (25 blocks of 40 trials). Overall accuracy, and perceptual sensitivity (d’), decreased significantly over the course of the experiment. This effect is consistent with the well-known vigilance decrement that occurs in tasks with long durations (Mackworth, 1948; Warm et al., 1996; Warm et al., 2008). Alenezi and Bindemann (2015) also found a significant shift in response bias over time. As the task progressed, participants became more likely to respond “match” to all trials. To the best of our knowledge, no one has yet investigated whether, and how, the face matching performance of human-algorithm teams changes over time. The overarching aim of the current experiment is to investigate whether the performance of human algorithm teams changes over the course of a “long” face matching task. Because the human will be asked to make the final identification decision, this question is more specifically about how human use of the algorithm’s decision changes over time. Of course, one of the benefits of AFR systems is that they do not suffer from time on task or fatigue effects. Carragher et al. (2024) reported that participants generally held more favourable attitudes toward the sAFR system after using it as a decision aid in a face matching task. On every trial of the current experiment, participants in the main experiment (sAFR condition) will submit two identification decisions – one unaided and one aided by the sAFR system. We expect that their unaided performance will decrease over time, as per Alenezi and Bindemann (2015). But based on Carragher et al. (2024), we expect that participants will show greater reliance on the sAFR system as the experiment progresses. Because the sAFR system will be given a level of accuracy that significantly exceeds the average participant (based on prior human accuracy data), this greater reliance is likely to show as an improvement in assisted accuracy over time. However, because we are expecting greater system reliance, we think it is unlikely the average participant will achieve a level of average assisted performance that exceeds that of the system alone (i.e., a collaborative performance gain) - which has not been seen in our previous work either (Carragher & Hancock, 2023; Carragher et al., 2024; Hua et al., 2025; Mueller et al., 2024). Finally, with this greater reliance, we expect that participants will be less likely to correct system errors as the experiment progresses. In addition to our main experimental condition (sAFR condition), we will also recruit a control condition to do the same long face matching task, but without assistance from a sAFR system at all.

items.title: Twenty-Five-Year Seroprevalence of HIV Infection Among Burn Admissions at a National Burns Referral Centre in Oman: A Retrospective Cross-Sectional Register Study, 1999–2024
items.abstract: Introduction Burn injury and HIV infection have important clinical and occupational-health implications. However, burn-unit HIV seroprevalence data have not previously been published from the Arabian Gulf. We aimed to estimate HIV seroprevalence among burn admissions to Oman's national burns referral centre over 25 years and describe patient characteristics and outcomes. Materials and Methods We conducted a retrospective cross-sectional register study of the unit's HIV-1/2 antigen/antibody screening register from October 1999 to December 2024. An admission was classified as reactive if any associated result was reactive; confirmed infection required repeat reactive/positive results during the same admission. The register shifted from qualitative negative/positive reporting, predominantly during 1999–2008, to quantitative signal-to-cutoff reporting, predominantly from 2010; manufacturer-specific assay details were not consistently available. Results Of 2,152 admission episodes, 1,705 (79.2%; 1,703 unique patients) had interpretable HIV results; 447 (20.8%) did not. Median age was 17 years, 61.1% were male, and 48.4% were younger than 15 years. TBSA was documented for 958/1,705 admissions (56.2%; median 19%, IQR 10–39%). Among these 958 admissions, in-hospital mortality increased across TBSA categories from 0.5% (<20%) to 5.4% (20–39%) and 36.2% (≥40%) (Cochran–Armitage trend test, p<0.001; Pearson χ²=235.5, df=2). One admission had confirmed HIV infection, giving a seroprevalence of 0.06% (95% CI 0.001–0.33%). Two additional admissions had unconfirmed reactive screens; including these gives an upper-bound estimate of 0.18% (95% CI 0.04–0.51%). Oman's modelled national prevalence is approximately 0.02% (0.2 per 1,000). Conclusion Confirmed HIV seroprevalence was very low and comparable with Oman's national estimate in this national referral population. Findings support careful interpretation of reactive screens and reflex confirmatory testing. The study was approved by the Khoula Hospital Ethical Board.

items.title: Understanding Clinician Engagement with AI in Radiology: Protocol for a Pre-Implementation Qualitative Study to Inform Learning-to-Defer System Design
items.abstract: This project is a qualitative study of clinical decision-making in chest X-ray (CXR) interpretation at Oxford University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust (OUH), a setting in which multiple AI tools have recently been evaluated and in which a Learning-to-defer (L2D) system is in development. It constitutes a case study of clinician engagement with AI in radiology. This sits within a broader project examining how cognitive mechanisms and system-level factors shape clinicians' engagement with AI tools across different stages of development, implementation, and use. At the radiology site, this work will inform the design of a prototype L2D system: a human–AI set-up in which the AI either makes a decision itself or routes (defers) it to a human, based on their respective past performance. Component A of this protocol addresses the question of how trust, advice-taking, and group decision-making operate within the CXR reporting pathway, and what sociotechnical conditions shape AI engagement in this setting. It will also explore the system attributes which influence the safe implementation of an L2D tool that is being developed for radiology. Component B of the protocol directly addresses questions related to the design requirements of the L2D system: what deferral format would clinicians accept, who should receive deferred cases, how should deferral decisions be presented, and what outcome criteria would constitute meaningful benefit? These questions require an understanding of the psychological mechanisms that clinicians rely on when engaging with AI tools, and of the clinical system in which clinicians work. Overall, the study aims to build the evidence base that responsible development and deployment of such a system will require. This way, the technical design of the L2D system can be grounded in an understanding of who makes decisions, how, under what conditions, and practically what meaningful benefit would look like in this setting. The analysis draws on theories of trust, advice-taking, and group decision-making, situated within sociotechnical frameworks for understanding healthcare work (Systems Engineering Initiative for Patient Safety [SEIPS] 2.0; nonadoption, abandonment, scale-up, spread, and sustainability [NASSS] framework).

items.title: Understanding data ecosystems: Conceptual foundations of the phenomenon
items.abstract: Abstract Data ecosystems are increasingly recognized as critical to digital supply chains as they enable firms to access, exchange, govern, and mobilize data for coordinated action. These complex sociotechnical networks enable diverse stakeholders to engage in generating, sharing, and processing data, thereby fostering value creation across various industries. Yet despite growing interest, literature still lacks a consolidated understanding of what constitutes a data ecosystem and how its core elements interrelate. To address these issues, the present study employs a multimethod research design comprising a systematic literature review and a case study involving eight data ecosystem actors. The findings identify four constitutive subsystems of the data ecosystem: stakeholders, infrastructure, data, and governance, along with their underlying components. The study identifies six interrelations among these components, showing that data ecosystems depend not only on the presence of core elements but also on the relationships among them. By integrating insights from prior literature with empirical evidence, the study develops a foundation for understanding data ecosystems. The paper contributes to information systems (IS) research by clarifying the sociotechnical structure of data ecosystems and by providing a basis for future theorizing on interorganizational data sharing, governance, and responsive digital supply chains.

items.title: Virtual Reality at the Threshold of Transformation: Paradigms, Empirical Benefits, and Systemic Limitations
items.abstract: Over the past two decades, Virtual Reality (VR) has evolved from an entertainment novelty to a fundamental medium for digital transformation in education, clinical medicine, industrial engineering, and public administration.Combining bibliometric mapping with a critical review of the literature, this paper summarizes the current state of the modern immersive ecosystem, examining its main operational domains, empirical benefits, systemic bottlenecks, and development trajectories.Our results indicate that VR significantly enhances procedural learning, diagnostic accuracy, and collaborative workflows through high-fidelity, risk-free simulations.Placing VR within the broader framework of Extended Reality (XR), we analyze its convergence with Artificial Intelligence, distributed cloud-edge topologies, the Internet of Things (IoT), and Digital Twins.Specifically, we assess how delivery architectures such as Virtual Reality as a Service (VRaaS) mitigate traditional hardware constraints, enabling scalable and concurrent deployment, while documenting the contributions of Romanian research groups in this field.Despite clear benefits in terms of cognitive engagement and operational cost efficiency, large-scale institutional adoption faces persistent challenges, including cybersickness, ergonomic limitations, infrastructure expenses, cybersecurity risks, and data privacy governance.Finally, this analysis highlights VR's transition to a ubiquitous digital tool, arguing that its long-term viability depends on responsible algorithmic design, robust edge infrastructures, and cross-platform interoperability.

items.title: When Experience Becomes Metric: Systemic Model of Distress in Intelligent Digital Environments (SMDIDE)
items.abstract: Abstract The disruptions generated by AI within production systems alter the human experience at work and outline the emergence of digital distress in contemporary labor environments. The model was developed through a conceptual methodology based on interdisciplinary synthesis, integrating sociotechnical studies, cognitive psychology, labor theory, and critical AI scholarship. As a result, the SM-DIDE model conceptualizes distress as a dynamic process that arises during human-machine interaction, where cognitive and technological overload is processed as cognitive demand through the functional articulation of six interdependent subsystems. The activation, modulation, and feedback among these subsystems explain the variability in the presentation, course, and trajectories of distress. Three subsystems describe the progression from the perception of cognitive and technological demand to the emergence of evolutionary trajectories. This progression is neither linear nor deterministic: it is modulated by the transversal subsystem of involuntary regulation and by the dysfunctional coping subsystem, both of which interact with the direct influence of the structural modulation subsystem to determine the load exerted on the worker during the interaction with AI. The model reframes distress as a process and directs research toward work environments centered on human experience, integrating domains rarely articulated together—cognitive, epistemic, affective, existential, and sociotechnical—and advancing toward a unified theory of digital distress.

items.title: When shifts matter for hybrid teams: The moderating role of location predictability.
items.abstract: In recent years, changes to the nature of work and evolving employee preferences have led to the rise of hybrid teams. In contrast to traditional teams, hybrid teams frequently shift between remote and face-to-face interaction. This structure raises new questions about how such dynamism impacts team engagement, an emergent state typically thought to develop under long periods of stability and face-to-face interaction. Drawing on the boundary transition theory of dynamic teamwork, we theorize that weekly downshifts in face-to-face interaction (i.e., relative decreases from the prior week) harm weekly team engagement and performance, but only for teams with lower levels of location predictability-an important yet understudied differentiator of hybrid team functioning. To test these ideas, we use a within-team, repeated-measures field survey design with a sample of hybrid sales teams at a large alcohol distributor in China. We surveyed 164 hybrid teams and their supervisors across 6 weeks (648 team-level weekly responses) to capture shifts in team work locations and examine their impact on weekly team engagement and performance. Results supported our hypotheses. By focusing on the role of weekly fluctuations in team structures and how location predictability shapes these effects, we advance our understanding of the unique and dynamic nature of hybrid teams. items.title: Where Does Accountability Lie in Deployed AI Systems? Using Cognitive Work Analysis to Address the Value-Alignment Problem
items.abstract: Increased use of Artificial Intelligence raises questions around mitigating unintended consequences. Technical perspectives on these questions lead to calls for “Responsible AI,” while regulatory perspectives lead to calls for increased human oversight. Neither perspective fully addresses the core issues surrounding accountability in the sociotechnical systems in which AI operates. Human oversight is a form of supervisory control, in which the role of the human is to monitor AI performance within defined constraints, and this requires consideration of who defines the constraints, where accountability lies when the constraints are exceeded, and how AI performance can be interpreted by human supervisors. For us, constraints correspond to system’s Values and a challenge lies in aligning system operations with these Values. We demonstrate the use of Work Domain Analysis to map purpose-related functions (i.e., activity performed in a sociotechnical system) to Values (weighted according to the functional purpose of the organization).

items.title: Work Environment Factors and Work Efficiency Among Filipino US Registered Nurses in Remote Utilization Management Roles in The United States Healthcare System
items.abstract: Remote Utilization Management has emerged as an alternative nursing role for Filipino United States Registered Nurses, yet evidence concerning their working conditions and efficiency remains limited. This study examined the relationship between work environment factors and work efficiency and developed an evidence-based training program. Methods: A quantitative descriptive-correlational design was used among 158 Filipino USRNs working in remote Utilization Management. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire measuring physical work environment, technological support, workload, organizational support, communication, work-life balance, leadership, productivity, accuracy, timeliness, decision making, and job performance. Frequency, percentage, mean, independent samples t test, analysis of variance, Welch’s analysis, and Pearson correlation were employed. Results: Respondents generally reported high levels of work environment and work efficiency. Physical work environment and technological support were the strongest workplace dimensions, while workload and work-life balance were comparatively lowest. Quality and accuracy emerged as the strongest efficiency dimension, whereas productivity was comparatively lowest. Work environment and efficiency differed significantly according to educational attainment, civil status, nursing experience, and remote Utilization Management experience, but not according to age or sex. All work environment dimensions had very strong positive relationships with productivity, accuracy, timeliness, decision making, and overall performance. Discussion: The findings indicate that favorable physical, technological, organizational, relational, and psychosocial conditions are integral to efficient remote nursing practice. The REMOTE-UM EXCEL Program was proposed to strengthen ergonomics, technology competence, workflow management, communication, evidence based decisions, leadership, psychological safety, and work-life boundaries. Organizations should implement integrated workplace interventions and evaluate their effects through longitudinal and performance-based measures to support sustained quality, employee well-being, and organizational effectiveness.

items.title: Workplace Violence, Psychosocial Risks and Mental Health Across Healthcare Professional Groups
items.abstract: Healthcare workers are exposed to workplace violence, yet the extent and nature of this exposure may differ considerably across professional groups. Psychosocial working conditions, including high work demands, emotional demands, working-time pressures and employment relations, may shape the conditions in which workplace violence occurs and is experienced. This study investigates psychosocial risks, workplace violence and symptoms of depression, anxiety and stress among nurses, physicians, healthcare assistants and administrative staff, and examines whether workplace violence is statistically associated with the relationship between psychosocial risks and these symptoms. A cross-sectional study was conducted with 289 Portuguese healthcare workers using three validated instruments: the Psychosocial Risk Factors Scale (INSAT_ERPS), the Aggression and Violence at Work Scale and the Depression Anxiety Stress Scales (DASS-21). Group differences were tested with Kruskal–Wallis tests, associations with Spearman correlations, and mediation and moderation analyses were performed using SPSS and the PROCESS macro. Results showed that workplace violence affected all professional groups but was more intense among nurses. Psychosocial risk was strongly associated with workplace violence, and this association did not differ across professional groups. However, neither psychosocial risks nor violence were associated with depression, anxiety or stress, and no statistically significant indirect association was observed. These findings highlight the importance of addressing workplace violence as an organizational and occupational health issue rather than a problem confined to specific professions.

items.title: YQX+: Benchmarking Probabilistic Modeling of Piano Performance Expression
items.abstract: Abstract A written music score specifies what notes should be played, but much of the musical meaning of a performance comes from how those notes are interpreted: pianists shape timing, dynamics, tempo, and articulation to communicate structure, style, and emotion. Modeling this expressive aspect of music matters for music education, digital performance rendering, and creative AI systems, and is difficult precisely because the same score admits many different but musically valid interpretations.In this paper, we present YQX+, a benchmarking framework for probabilistic modeling of expressive piano performance. YQX+ shifts the focus from demonstrating a single rendering system to comparing how different models capture the expressive variation observed in human performance. To make that comparison possible, it fixes the prediction task, a shared multi-scale contextual feature representation, and a common evaluation protocol, so that model families are trained and compared on equal footing. Given a symbolic score, every model in the suite predicts the same note-level expressive parameters, including beat period, velocity, timing deviation, and articulation ratio, from features that capture local note context, harmonic texture, phrase structure, and score markings. The suite takes the original YQX Gaussian mixture model (GMM) as its reference point and extends it to XGBoost, variational autoencoders, and conditional flow-matching models.To support perceptual evaluation, we also introduce PerformanceMOS, a data-driven estimator of perceived expressive quality and performance skill from symbolic piano performances. Experiments show that larger-capacity XGBoost and \((\beta)\)-VAE models achieve lower timing and articulation errors than prior baselines, including DExter and VirtuosoNet, and obtain the highest predicted mean opinion scores (MOS). These findings establish YQX+ as a systematic benchmark for probabilistic modeling of piano performance expression, with PerformanceMOS providing a scalable proxy for human listening evaluation. The code, trained models, and evaluation scripts are available at \texttt{https://github.com/kkwsts/YQX-Plus}.

items.title: A Chatbot Served 10 Ways: An Experimental Analysis of the Quality of Chatbot Responses Powered by Large Language Models
items.abstract: This study reports on an evaluation of responses from 10 custom-developed chatbots to assess how chatbot answer evaluation might best be done for benchmarking and real-world environments. We asked the same 16 questions to 10 configurations of our chatbot and compared the quality of the responses provided with two key metrics: how well the chatbots’ responses scored on the Flesch-Kincaid readability test, and how well they held up to scrutiny from technical communication experts. We show how the Flesch-Kincaid readability test can be misleading and should not be considered as a comprehensive measurement when it comes to evaluating the output generated by AI models. We discuss the limitations of the Flesch-Kincaid readability test and preview our current work integrating the ISO 24495-1 Plain Language standards into the assessment of AI-driven chatbots.

items.title: Age-Inclusive Dynamic Wayfinding Design for Large Transportation Hubs: An Experimental Study of Information Volume and Scrolling Cycle
items.abstract: The proliferation of Variable Message Signs (VMS) in large transportation hubs is driven by their core capability to flexibly address complex and changing conditions in vehicular and pedestrian traffic. This capability allows for real-time guidance that alleviates congestion and optimizes the use of space. The complexity and rapid dynamics of VMS information can exceed older adults’ cognitive processing capacities, hindering their ability to rapidly locate critical information and comprehend travel instructions. These difficulties subsequently lead to inefficient wayfinding, increased decision-making errors, and heightened frustration. To address this issue, this study examines the effects of two key dynamic design parameters—information volume and scrolling cycle—on wayfinding efficiency and attention allocation across different age groups. Grounded in theories of visual perception and information entropy, a controlled eye-tracking experiment was conducted that combined behavioral performance measures with gaze data. The findings reveal an effective balance between information volume and scrolling cycle. This specific combination helps reduce performance differences across age groups: it maintains high interaction efficiency for younger users while significantly enhancing information acquisition for older adults. Furthermore, it mitigated the over-capture of attention by dynamic information. Based on these empirical results, we propose a design strategy for VMS that integrates dynamic information parameters with static interface principles. This strategy applies inclusive human-computer interaction (HCI) principles to the domain of dynamic public interfaces. Moving beyond foundational universal design elements (e.g., typography, color contrast), it positions empirically optimized dynamic information quantification and presentation rhythm as core design dimensions. This research provides empirical evidence and practical design guidance for optimizing intelligent wayfinding systems in complex public environments, contributing to more inclusive and effective human-computer interactions.

items.title: Algorithmic Management as a Double-Edged Form of Digital Work Design: Job Demands, Autonomy and Employee Outcomes across 35 European Countries
items.abstract: Abstract Computer-based managerial systems are part of the digital infrastructure of work, with potential implications for employee demands and discretion. Drawing on Job Demands-Resources theory, this study examines task allocation, work scheduling and performance monitoring as distinct functions and their parallel indirect associations with engagement and intention to quit through work intensity and autonomy. Weighted least squares mean- and variance-adjusted structural equation models were estimated for 26,504 employees in 35 European countries using the 2024 European Working Conditions Survey. The measures capture reported computer involvement rather than verified artificial intelligence capabilities. Engagement and autonomy were modelled as latent factors, and quit intention as an ordinal outcome. All three practices were positively associated with work intensity. Task allocation was positively associated with autonomy, whereas monitoring was negatively associated with autonomy; scheduling’s negative autonomy association was less robust to contextual fixed effects. Task allocation showed opposing indirect engagement associations through intensity and autonomy, whereas monitoring showed negative associations through both pathways. Intensity-related indirect associations with quit intention were consistently positive, while autonomy-related indirect associations were not statistically significant in the primary or fixed-effects models. Sensitivity analyses supported the main directional patterns, while exploratory country diagnostics indicated incomplete measurement invariance and heterogeneous slopes. The findings inform the evaluation of digital management by distinguishing functions associated with greater demands and greater autonomy from those associated with greater demands and reduced autonomy. The cross-sectional design does not establish causal mediation or uniform cross-country relationships.

items.title: Black pragmatism and organization studies
items.abstract: I argue for Black pragmatism’s usefulness to organization studies by intervening in debates about the normative foundations of stakeholder theory. Tracing three braided themes within Black pragmatism (tragicomic hope, critical temper, and democratic faith), I show how they both illuminate neglected aspects of the pragmatist themes of inquiry, abduction, and community that have influenced organization studies and extend those concepts to open new avenues of inquiry. I suggest that Black pragmatism reveals how the libertarian assumptions of stakeholder theory are inconsistent with its pragmatist commitments, and that this weakness even applies to recent attempts to center stakeholder theory upon marginalized stakeholders.

items.title: Bounded Adaptive Agency in Intelligent Products: Designing Scope, Control, and Non-Intrusion in Human-AI Interaction
items.abstract: Everyday intelligent products increasingly use adaptive components whose actions are constrained by capability, context, uncertainty, and privacy. We introduce bounded adaptive agency, a design framework for making these constraints understandable and controllable. Study 1 interviewed 28 designers and related specialists, identifying four interdependent boundaries: capability, deployment, agency, and interruption. Study 2 tested a boundary-oriented design canvas in a controlled concept-generation task with 54 participants, examining how it shaped early decisions about scope, uncertainty, autonomy, recovery, and interruption. items.title: Clarification Design for E-Commerce Service Chatbots: Effects of Interaction Mode and Personalization on Task Efficiency and User Experience
items.abstract: This study examines how clarification interaction mode and personalization level jointly influence task efficiency and user experience in e-commerce service encounters. In a 2 × 3 between-subjects experiment, 60 participants were randomly assigned to six conditions and completed five after-sales tasks. Objective performance was assessed by completion time; subjective evaluations included perceived warmth, perceived competence, perceived privacy risk, interaction satisfaction, and cognitive effort. The five completion-time outcomes were analyzed using MANOVA, followed by exploratory task-specific two-way ANOVAs. Selection mode was associated with shorter completion times in each of the five service scenarios and with higher perceived competence and interaction satisfaction than open-input clarification. Exploratory follow-up analyses identified statistically significant personalization effects in some scenarios, and personalization level was associated only with perceived competence among subjective measures. Because task was not modeled as a within-subject factor, these findings do not establish that personalization effects differed statistically across tasks.

items.title: Comparative Judgments of Waiting Time across Smartphone Countdown Formats
items.abstract: Numerical countdown formats may influence comparative judgments of waiting time. We compared six integer-only and decimal countdown formats on participants’ own smartphones. Experiment 1 measured paired judgments of countdown duration, whereas Experiment 2 measured paired judgments of site loading speed in a web-application-like task. One-decimal-place displays tended to receive longer or slower judgments than several alternatives. In the 10-second condition, formats with two to five decimal places received shorter or faster judgments than integer-only and one-decimal-place formats in both experiments, although differences within the two-to-five-decimal group varied between experiments. These results describe relative judgments among the tested formats, not an absolute reduction in perceived waiting time. Because decimal precision and updating behavior were not manipulated independently, the findings concern the formats as implemented rather than digit count alone. They provide conditional guidance for comparing countdown formats in interface design.

items.title: Consider the Dashboard: Exploring a visual medium of datafication
items.abstract: Dashboards are central to contemporary organizations aiming to ‘datafy’ decision making and management practices. As one of the primary media through which people engage with digital data in organizational contexts, dashboards shape how data is accessed and perceived. Despite their ubiquity, there is limited understanding of how dashboards mediate data visibility and influence observers’ perceptions of the data. Drawing on theories of mediation and diagrammatics, this paper analyzes the ‘generic form’ shared by all dashboards. It then identifies the modes of observation encouraged by dashboards, revealing how they position their observers. While grounded in theoretical arguments, the analysis incorporates empirical examples from a study on the datafication of Human Resource Management. The paper makes two key contributions. It emphasizes the critical role of visual forms in datafication processes, and it highlights the organizational implications of the use of a specific kind of visual medium: the dashboard.

items.title: Counting crashes is not enough: developing an exposure-based high risk network for e-scooter safety
items.abstract: Shared e-scooters are now common in urban transportation, but safety planning remains limited by a lack of exposure-based, spatially detailed crash risk measures. This study applied an exposure-based approach to identify high-risk e-scooter corridors in Nashville, Tennessee, combining 92 police-reported, motor-vehicle-involved e-scooter crashes with trip-kilometer exposure data over a 45-month period. Crashes were assigned to corridors by rider direction of travel, and rates were calculated per 100,000 vehicle kilometers traveled (VKT) citywide and by corridor. Across more than five million e-scooter kilometers of exposure, the citywide crash rate was 1.84 per 100,000 VKT, and 82.6% of crashes occurred at intersections or driveways. The 25 corridors accounted for 75.0% of crashes and 70.9% of VKT, with a combined rate (1.94 per 100,000 VKT) statistically indistinguishable from the rest of Nashville (1.58; p = 0.34). Corridor-level rates were nonetheless heterogeneous (chi-square = 96.17, df = 24, p < 0.001), with unadjusted rates ranging from 0.69 to 24.49 crashes per 100,000 VKT; empirical Bayes shrinkage reduced this spread to roughly 3.7-fold. Three corridors, Shelby Avenue, 21st Avenue, and West End Avenue, exceeded the citywide rate individually, with the first two remaining significant after correction for multiple comparisons. Exposure-adjusted corridor rates gave a different picture of risk than crash counts alone: citywide averages concealed substantial street-level variation, supporting corridor-level exposure measures as a screening tool for micromobility safety, though individual designations remain exploratory rather than confirmatory. These results let agencies combine trip and crash data to target safety investment at high-risk corridors.

items.title: Does Higher Algorithm Adaptability Increase Usage Intention Among Professional Users? A Dual-Path Mechanism Moderated by Task Type
items.abstract: As adaptive algorithms permeate professional settings, does higher algorithm adaptability enhance professional users’ usage intention? Drawing on Self-Determination Theory, three complementary studies were conducted: secondary analysis of Doubao AI-assistant reviews (N = 409), a between-subjects experiment with 190 participants simulating language-editing tasks, and a replication with 193 university faculty in authentic teaching contexts. Results showed that adaptability enhanced usage intention in subjective tasks but attenuated it in objective tasks. Mechanistically, higher adaptability promotes usage intention by strengthening users’ confidence in their ability to perform the task (task self-efficacy); however, in objective tasks it also erodes perceived transparency—a precondition for professionals to verify and take accountability for algorithmic outputs—thereby dampening usage intention. These opposing pathways jointly weaken the effect in objective tasks. This study extends algorithm-attitude theory by treating adaptability as an inherent design attribute, clarifying its dual pathways and boundary conditions, with practical implications for professional AI design.

items.title: Effects of Steering Strategies and Posture for 360° Object Selection in Virtual Reality
items.abstract: Most virtual reality (VR) object-selection research restricts targets to the user’s initial field of view, thereby lacking ecological validity for omnidirectional applications. Addressing this limitation, our study investigates 360° object selection in VR, evaluating human performance, workload, and usability across varying postures (standing vs. seated) and steering strategies (physical body movement vs. controller). Through a human-subject experiment with 36 participants encompassing 24 azimuth and three inclination angles, we provide novel empirical evidence on full-surround target acquisition in VR. Results also reveal that physical body movement is faster and more usable when standing, while controller steering yields stable selection times across postures and reduces workload when seated. This finding suggests that optimal VR steering strategies are intrinsically linked to the user’s physical posture. Ultimately, this work advances our understanding of full-surround target acquisition in VR, contributing to empirical guidelines for designing adaptive, posture-aware spatial interaction techniques in omnidirectional virtual environments.

items.title: Elite Strength and Conditioning Coaches as First-Line Users of Sports-Science Technology: Dashboard Workarounds in Time-Constrained Decision-Making
items.abstract: Elite strength and conditioning (S&C) coaches occupy a critical but underexamined position as first-line users of sports-science technology, responsible for translating raw athlete-monitoring data into immediate training decisions. Through seven semi-structured interviews with elite S & C coaches across NCAA Division I, professional, and Olympic contexts, we identify four recurring breakdowns in their daily data work: fragmented vendor ecosystems, metric overload, scale and staffing constraints and staff turnover. Static mockup elicitation during interviews revealed a consistent preference for simple, interpretable interfaces that foreground selected metrics and concise explanations over dense data displays. We position elite S&C coaches as a distinct user group whose needs are poorly served by current systems, and propose four design priorities: integration stability, selective metrics with contextual explanation, scale-aware views, and governance continuity, to guide future coach-facing sports-science interface design.
