items.title: Empirical Analysis of Driver Behavior at Uncontrolled Midblock Crosswalks: Influence of Bike Lane Buffer Types
items.abstract: Abstract At unsignalized midblock crosswalks (UMCs), visual obstructions created by bike lane buffers can substantially affect drivers’ pedestrian detection and yielding behavior. However, limited evidence is available regarding how different types of bike lane buffers influence driving performance through changes in visual attention and cognitive workload. To address this issue, four representative bike lane buffer scenarios—Lawn, Railing, Bush, and Tree—were developed in a driving simulation environment. Vehicle operation parameters and eye-tracking data were collected simultaneously to investigate drivers’ behavioral and visual responses while approaching a crosswalk. The results showed that highly obstructive buffers significantly delayed pedestrian detection and weakened drivers’ early risk perception. In the Bush and Tree scenarios, pedestrians were detected at distances of only about 18 m from the crosswalk, representing a reduction of more than 40% compared with the low-obstruction conditions. As a consequence, drivers exhibited lower terminal braking speeds, higher maximum deceleration rates, and more abrupt braking maneuvers. The mean braking initiation distance in the Bush and Tree scenarios was approximately 48 m, which was more than 10 m shorter than that observed under the Lawn and Railing conditions. Eye-tracking analyses further revealed that highly obstructive environments significantly increased fixation duration on roadside areas while reducing the effective visual search range. In addition, the proportions of saccades and blinks decreased to approximately 3%, whereas the coefficient of variation of pupil diameter increased to 0.23, indicating elevated cognitive workload and mental stress. These findings demonstrate that visual obstructions associated with bike lane buffers can adversely affect drivers’ hazard perception, visual search behavior, and braking responses. The study provides empirical evidence to support the safety evaluation and design optimization of bike lane buffers near unsignalized midblock crosswalks.

items.title: Evaluating a Hardware-Free Grasp-Realistic Pseudo-Haptic Configuration for Fine Motor Object Insertion in Virtual Reality
items.abstract: Precise object manipulation in virtual reality (VR) remains challenging without haptic feedback. Haptic devices can improve motor performance but are often expensive, complex, and unsuitable for some tasks. We evaluate a composite pseudo-haptic configuration combining motion delay with realistic finger-object alignment to support precise object insertion. In a within-subject study, 25 participants grasped objects of different shapes and sizes and inserted them into matching holes. Compared with a default VR hand-grasp baseline, the pseudo-haptic configuration significantly reduced task completion times and collision durations with higher usability, lower workload, and higher presence. We performed a cross-study comparison between hardware-free and glove-based configurations using a prior haptic-glove study’s raw data with identical task structure, objects, and evaluation metrics. Results suggest the pseudo-haptic configuration achieved shorter task completion times and collision durations. Overall, the findings suggest that hardware-free pseudo-haptic configurations are promising for precise VR manipulation while reducing reliance on specialized haptic hardware.

items.title: GoldMind: a teacher-centred knowledge management system for higher education – lessons from iterative design
items.abstract: Designing Knowledge Management Systems (KMSs) for higher education requires addressing complex human–technology interactions, especially where staff turnover and changing roles create challenges for reusing knowledge. While advances in process mining and Generative AI enable new ways of designing features to support knowledge management, existing KMSs often overlook the realities of educators' workflows, leading to low adoption and limited impact. This paper presents findings from a two-year human-centred design study with 108 higher education teachers, examining iterative co-design and evaluation of GoldMind – a KMS supporting in-the-flow knowledge management during digital teaching tasks. Through three design–evaluation cycles, we examined teachers' task-evaluations and how feedback informed refinements. Insights are synthesised across three themes: (1) Technology Lessons from user interaction data, (2) Design Considerations shaped by co-design and usability testing, and (3) Human Factors, including cognitive load and knowledge behaviours, analysed using Epistemic Network Analysis (in the last iteration). This study demonstrates that embedding human-centred, workflow-integrated KMSs can improve task efficiency, reduce cognitive load, and support knowledge reuse, while shaping educators' knowledge management behaviours through context-aware and proactive support. However, findings are based on a single-institution, controlled evaluation, limiting generalisability and requiring longitudinal, in-the-wild studies to assess adoption and impact.

items.title: Healing As Organizing in Solidarity Spaces: An Affective Perspective on Post-disaster Recovery
items.abstract: This paper examines how community-led solidarity initiatives enable healing in the aftermath of disaster. Drawing on a two-year qualitative study in post-explosion Beirut, it explores how solidarity spaces function as relational structures of repair – sites where material response and affective recovery are not separate processes but mutually constitutive ones. While post-disaster organizing research has emphasized resource mobilization and agility, and disaster studies has identified the importance of community-led recovery, neither has fully explored how organizing enables healing to unfold collectively. Addressing this gap, the study makes two contributions. First, it reframes solidarity spaces as generative holding environments: relational infrastructures that simultaneously contain suffering and enable the emergence of new social arrangements. Second, it conceptualizes healing as organizing: a distributed, collective, and enacted process through which communities transform suffering into agency. Healing, in this account, is not an individual psychological process nor an outcome that follows organizing; it is the very practice through which recovery unfolds, as participants become agents of their own material and affective transformation through acts of solidarity.

items.title: LLM-Generated Design Problems for Assessing Higher-Order Thinking in Project-Based Learning
items.abstract: Project-based learning (PjBL) is common in computing education, but traditional assessments of PjBL often fail to capture higher-order thinking (HOT), especially in transfer contexts. This study introduces ''design problems'' (DPs): concise, scenario-based prompts that require applying project concepts in new situations, to address this gap. We examined instructor perceptions, the ability of large language models (LLMs) to generate DPs, and student experiences. Surveys of 31 instructors, evaluation of 80 LLM-generated DPs, and student performance data showed that while instructors value DPs, creation effort is a barrier. LLMs helped by producing high-quality prompts with strong expert agreement. Students rated DPs from different LLMs similarly, and their performance on DP tasks showed negligible correlation with traditional project grades, suggesting DPs may capture distinct aspects of HOT. Keystroke data also suggested deeper cognitive engagement of students through planning and revision behaviors. Overall, DPs appear to be a useful complement to traditional assessments, especially in situations where AI use or collaboration may undermine individual learning.

items.title: Occupational Exposure to N,N-Dimethylformamide and Hepatotoxicity among Synthetic Leather Workers in Bangladesh: Implications for Workplace Health and Labour Law Compliance
items.abstract: Abstract Purpose : N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF) is a polar aprotic solvent that is extensively used in the production of synthetic leather, polyurethane products, resins, adhesives and surface coatings. Potential sources of occupational exposures are mixing, formulation, coating, solvent transfer, cleaning, maintenance, and spill-response. DMF may be inhaled and absorbed through intact skin, which means that total internal dose for a particular worker may be underestimated by only measuring DMF in the air. Liver is a known target organ of DMF toxicity, and reports of increased liver enzymes and, less frequently, clinically significant liver injury have been reported in workers occupationally exposed to DMF. Increases in liver-function tests, however, are non-specific and can occur in people who drink too much alcohol and/or are obese, and/or may be caused by metabolic disease associated with steatotic liver disease, viral hepatitis, certain medicines (prescribed or not) or other exposures that may occur at work. Therefore, a comprehensive evaluation of possible liver damage from DMF should include exposure history, workplace monitoring, biological monitoring, repeated clinical evaluations, and the careful consideration of other causes of liver damage. Objective : The aim of this study is to find the relationship between DMF exposure and liver injury in the workers working in the synthetic leather, polyurethane, resin and surface-coating industries. It will consider exposure by inhalation and skin contact, estimate internal exposure as measured by urinary markers, review liver-function patterns as they change over time, determine if another source of liver injury or exposure may have occurred, and determine if a failure of workplace controls or medical surveillance could have led to exposure. The results will help to inform evidence-based occupational-health and medico-legal decisions about the possibility and level of occupational contribution to liver disease. Methods : An occupational-health study using a mixed-methods approach will be conducted with workers who may be at risk for DMF, such as mixers, formulators, coating operators, solvent-transfer workers, cleaners, maintenance workers, and waste-handling workers. A standardised occupational history will document job titles, length of employment, work patterns, frequency of tasks, use of DMF containing products, past chemical exposures, spillages, symptoms, hygiene practices and use and suitability of personal protective equipment (PPE). Task specific workplace exposure assessments will be carried out and personal air sampling will be used, wherever possible, especially during transfer, mixing, coating, cleaning and maintenance activities. The results of the air-monitoring will be evaluated against relevant occupational exposure concentrations with an understanding that an exposure below the airborne concentration limit does not mean there is no significant dermal absorption. The dermal exposure potential will be evaluated by conducting facility observations and interviews with workers, which will include direct hands-on contact with the material, use of contaminated gloves and clothing, gloves used, gloves replaced, local exhaust ventilation, housekeeping, spill control, washing facility, training, and working practices. The urinary concentrations of N-methylformamide (NMF) and N-acetyl-S-(N-methylcarbamoyl)cysteine (AMCC) will be measured for internal DMF exposure. These are markers of systemic exposure from all routes of exposure including inhalation and skin contact. Ideally, urine samples will be collected at the end of shift and end of work week, or at other suitable times depending on the toxicokinetic properties of the biomarker. Urine dilutions, e.g. creatinine, specific gravity etc., will be corrected and results interpreted taking into account the timing of the sample, the analytical procedure and available biological guidance values. Serum alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT), alkaline phosphatase (ALP) levels, bilirubin, albumin and international normalised ratio (INR) will be measured at regular intervals. These tests will assist in the identification of hepatocellular, cholestatic or mixed liver injury patterns and be useful in identifying transient, persistent or progressive liver injuries. Symptoms such as fatigue, nausea, abdominal discomfort, jaundice, pruritus and constitutional symptoms will also be recorded. Systematic assessment of potential confounding factors and alternative diagnosis. Alcohol intake, BMI, presence of diabetes, metabolic disease, pre-existing liver disease, other hepatotoxic chemicals and drug or supplement use will be recorded. Investigations may consist of a hepatology specialist review, abdominal ultrasound and hepatitis B and C testing, where clinically appropriate and consented to. There will be a structured medico-legal review, combining evidence from 4 domains – exposure, biological plausibility, individual clinical disease and duty of care. Occupational history and occupational monitoring will support the results of urinary biomarkers as evidence of internal exposure. The adequacy of engineering controls, local exhaust ventilation, training, spill management, hazard communication and medical surveillance will be taken into account in the duty of care assessment. Challenging with the drug after a possible hepatotoxic reaction will not take place. Expected Results : The study will not pre-judge causation as there is currently no data. It is anticipated to see if the workers with high overall or task specific exposure would have higher levels of urinary NMF and AMCC, and if these workers would have more frequent and persistent liver-test abnormalities. It will also be evaluated if liver enzymes improve if DMF exposure is reduced or eliminated, if follow up is available. Importantly, the analysis will differentiate isolated elevations of enzymes from a pattern of occupationally related disease. Conclusions :Concurring inhalational and dermal exposure to DMF is an occupational-health hazard that can be prevented. Task-based exposure assessment, urinary biomarkers, serial liver tests, clinical differential diagnosis and structured medico-legal analysis is a better approach for assessing possible occupational hepatotoxicity than liver enzymes alone. Decisions regarding the possibility, probability and highly probable occupational contribution will be based on the overall evidence and distinct from legal liability.PPE, training, spillage or medical surveillance had a significant impact on the workers.

items.title: Organizational responses to near-miss reporting and perceived organizational support among Japanese workers: a longitudinal cohort study
items.abstract: Near-miss events in the workplace serve as important signals for occupational accident prevention, and organizational responses to near-miss reports may influence employees’ perceived organizational support (POS). the association between organizational response patterns to near-miss reports and POS has not been sufficiently examined. This longitudinal study used data from an online cohort study of Japanese workers conducted at baseline (March 2023) and follow-up (December 2023). The analysis included 1,168 non-managerial workers who had experienced at least one near-miss event. Participants were categorized into four groups based on reporting behavior and the adequacy of organizational responses: reporting with adequate response, reporting with partial response, reporting with no response (reference), and no reporting. Associations between response patterns and POS at follow-up were examined using linear regression analysis. Employees in the reporting with adequate response (B = 2.16, 95% CI: 0.71–3.61) and reporting with partial response (B = 1.68, 95% CI: 0.12–3.23) groups showed significantly higher POS at follow-up compared with the reporting with no response group. The no reporting group also showed significantly higher POS (B = 1.63, 95% CI: 0.13–3.12). No significant moderating effect of company size was observed. These findings suggest that the quality of organizational responses to near-miss reports is associated with POS regardless of company size. Employees who reported near-miss events but received no organizational response showed the lowest POS, even lower than those who did not report. These findings highlight the importance of adequate follow-up and communication after near-miss reporting.

items.title: Patience and Organization Studies: Festina lente
items.abstract: Modern organizations often valorize speed and immediacy, treating acceleration as the dominant temporal logic of organizational life. Challenging this logic remains difficult, however, because organization studies lacks a well-developed conceptual language for alternative ways of engaging with time. We propose patience as one such alternative. Building on recent work on Eigenzeit, we argue that organizations can partially uncouple from external temporal pressures and develop forms of relative temporal autonomy that enable the orchestration of differentiated temporalities. While Eigenzeit highlights how organizations establish and sustain a temporality of their own amid complex temporal demands, less attention has been paid to the pacing through which this temporality is enacted in everyday organizational life. We therefore foreground pacing as the practical means by which organizations enact and sustain their own temporality. Within this context, patience emerges as a particular mode of pacing grounded in purposeful deceleration. To make this mode of pacing analytically visible, we identify four manifestations of organizational patience: waiting, restraining, forbearing, and persisting. Drawing on insights from the sociology of time, organization studies, and philosophy, we show how these manifestations represent distinct ways of pacing organizational activities by holding time open, delaying intervention, staying with difficulty, and sustaining engagement over time. By reframing patience as a distinctive mode of pacing rather than passive inactivity, we show how organizations cultivate and sustain an Eigenzeit through practices that contribute to the orchestration of competing temporal demands. This perspective advances organization studies by illuminating how temporal orchestration is accomplished through everyday organizational interactions and how patience enables organizations to sustain resilience and meaningful engagement in the face of acceleration pressures.

items.title: Physiological Correlates of Passenger-Facing HMI Communication in Automated Driving
items.abstract: Passenger-facing vehicle interfaces must inform without disrupting non-driving activities. This study related HMI communication during fully automated driving to passenger physiology and interaction quality during concurrent reading. Twenty-six participants completed a no-communication Baseline drive and one HMI drive with abstract auditory-tactile cues (Simple) or synthesised speech (Extended); 24 contributed physiological data. Electrodermal activity (EDA) was the primary measure, with User Experience Questionnaire ratings. Because HMI variant was assigned between participants, participant-level analyses provided primary condition inference. Mean EDA was lower in both HMI conditions than Baseline, but no contrast was statistically supported (Simple–Baseline −73.1, 95% CI [−160.3, 14.0], p = 0.092; Extended–Baseline −44.7, p = 0.296; Extended–Simple 28.4, p = 0.614). No UEQ scale survived multiplicity correction. Segment-level mixed-effects models (803 segments) reproduced this ordering with narrower intervals reflecting repeated observations, not independent assignments. Participant-level contrasts matched the unit of assignment; segment-level models characterised temporal physiological variation.

items.title: Posture in practice: heightened awareness of surgical resident ergonomics
items.abstract: Abstract Background Ergonomics is an often-overlooked component of operative education. Early intervention can protect residents from physical stress and long-term musculoskeletal injury. Our aim is to evaluate residents during a simulated suturing exercise and assess the impact of self-evaluation on ergonomics. Methods Following informed consent, surgical residents performed a simulated complex wound closure, blinded to the study’s focus. Following initial closure, residents reviewed their videos with an ergonomic self-assessment guide, repeated the exercise, and completed a post-survey. Representative video clips were analyzed to measure elbow, spine, and neck angles. Standard angles were defined as 90–110° for elbow, < 10° for spine, and < 25° for neck. Results Twenty residents participated across four post-graduate years (PGY): five PGY-4, four PGY-3, four PGY-2, and seven PGY-1. Across all participants, we found significant reduction in spine (12.5° vs 5.1°, p = 0.016) and neck (58.5° vs 46.4°, p = 0.004) angle during the second exercise, but no difference in elbow angle (102.7° vs 101.7°, p = 0.744). The post-survey revealed most residents think about their ergonomics in the operating room at least weekly (75%) and feel physical strain (95%). All residents (100%) reported improved awareness of ergonomics and perceived transferability to the clinical setting. Discussion Our study demonstrated a resident self-assessment of ergonomics led to significant improvement in spinal and neck angles in a simulated exercise with increased awareness of operative ergonomics and perceived transferability to the clinical setting. These findings support integration of ergonomic education early in surgical training to help reduce physical strain and promote operative longevity.

items.title: Self-Employment and Well-Being Across Countries: A Longitudinal Replication and Extension
items.abstract: Nearly hundred studies in different times and places have documented that self-employed people report higher levels of subjective well-being than employed people. This “entrepreneurship well-being premium” is typically interpreted causally—"being your own boss" enhances well-being via more autonomy, favorable work design, and basic psychological need fulfillment. Yet, most of the evidence so far is cross-sectional, explanations fragmented across different theoretical mechanisms while rigorous tests distinguishing causation from selection are rather rare. We address this gap by first mapping five theoretical mechanisms—(1) procedural utility, (2) job demands-resources, (3) self-determination, (4) person–environment fit, and (5) selection on stable traits—into distinct stages of the causal process, further deriving discriminating predictions about each mechanism. In turn, using three waves of the Midlife in the United States (MIDUS) survey and two waves from the Global Flourishing study, we evaluate these competing predictions with a battery of converging tests, including cross-section analyses, individual fixed-effects models, and pre-transition analyses.

items.title: Street Fights and Court Battles: Incumbent mobilization and the timing of regulatory bans against platform entrants
items.abstract: In this paper, we examine how incumbent-led mobilization against Uber’s platform entry in Europe relates to regulatory bans, public attention, and consumer-side uptake. Combining hand-coded data on taxi-sector tactics and frames with first regulatory bans, Uber app downloads, and Google search interest across 22 European countries from 2012 to 2020, we identify a differentiated temporal pattern. Private tactics are strongly associated with first-ban hazard in the short window following mobilization, whereas lawsuits are positively associated over a longer window. The frames incumbents deploy also matter: legitimacy-challenge frames portraying UberPop as incompatible with lawful and fair competition are more consistently associated with bans than compliance-dispute frames focused on tax or labor obligations. At the same time, private tactics and lawsuits coincide with immediate increases in app downloads and Google search interest, indicating an attention spillover from incumbent contestation. Lawsuit-related download elevations display marginally greater persistence than those associated with private tactics, although this difference is not stronger early after entry. Taken together, the findings show that incumbent mobilization in platform markets can be associated with regulatory bans and consumer-side uptake of the entrants they seek to exclude at the same time. The results establish temporal association, although the direction of influence within this process cannot be isolated.

items.title: The AGI power dilemma and the illusion of safety with humans in the loop
items.abstract: Avoiding loss-of-control events will be key to industry and society as AI technology is employed in various critical processes. In this article, we assess a hypothetical instability situation of an AGI − a singularity event − from a safety science standpoint. We present one way to describe the process of how a real time Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) in its interaction with the environment may set it in a runaway condition. Our goal is clarifying general and structural control issues of strong real time AI for design, safeguarding and legislation. In cybernetics, instability and hence, the risk of loss-of-control, is a core trait of all highly adaptive systems. Such adaptive behavior can manifest as radical reframing – a pivotal process of a system that enables it to solve very hard challenges, and which requires it to redefine its core concepts, goals, values, plans and procedures. What emerges is the AGI power dilemma ; a double-bind between performance and controllability of a real time system. We discuss the consequences for human control of AGI and prospects for safeguarding when optimizing for power and speed. Moreover, we conclude that the human in the loop approach gives an illusion of safety when the AI is optimized for power.

items.title: The AI Metacognitive Calibration Paradox: An Inverted-U Relationship Between User Self-Monitoring and Human–AI Collaborative Performance
items.abstract: A persistent puzzle in human-computer interaction (HCI) is that AI training often fails to improve performance in AI-assisted tasks. This study introduces AI Metacognitive Calibration (AIMC), capturing users’ self-reported monitoring and adaptive regulation of cognitive engagement with AI systems. Using a sequential mixed-methods design (interviews with 24 knowledge workers followed by a survey of 289 professionals), we develop and validate the AIMC scale. Confirmatory factor analysis confirmed three first-order reflective dimensions: Monitoring Awareness (MA), Critical Evaluation (CE), and Adaptive Regulation (AR). Polynomial regression revealed a pattern consistent with an inverted-U association between AIMC and human–AI collaborative performance (HAICP), with performance peaking at moderate AIMC levels. Task complexity and AI system transparency moderated the location of the performance peak. Users with insufficient AIMC over-rely on AI output; users with excessive AIMC incur metacognitive overload. Findings challenge the “more training is better” assumption and reframe AI interface design toward calibration support.

items.title: The Interplay Between Individual Trait and Contextual Factors in Predicting Media Multitasking
items.abstract: The ubiquity of media multitasking and its negative effects on task performance underscore the importance of understanding what drives this behavior. While theoretical models propose that media multitasking arises from an interplay between individual trait and contextual factors, little research has directly examined it from this perspective. Across two studies, we explored the joint role of these factors in media multitasking. Study 1 examined whether relations between in-study media multitasking and individual traits in attention, self-regulation, and real-world media multitasking tendencies differed based on the contextual variable of task difficulty. Individual trait and contextual factors interacted when predicting media multitasking; however, results may have been affected by engagement with activities unrelated to the experimental content. Study 2 investigated the stability of multitasking behaviors and their associations with individual traits across two timepoints. Media multitasking was moderately correlated across sessions and did not consistently correlate with individual traits. It was, however, associated with greater enjoyment of the secondary media. Our findings suggest that media multitasking and its relations with trait measures are highly context-dependent, such that researchers studying media multitasking should carefully consider its sensitivity to context.

items.title: Understanding steering behaviors in paths with non-linear width changes
items.abstract: Steering through width-changing paths is fundamental in graphical user interface (GUI) tasks such as lasso selection. Researchers in ergonomics have modelled movement times by path shape, but most studies examined only linear width changes. We investigated the generalisability of the Steering Law by measuring movement times in paths where the width changes according to exponential, quadratic, and sigmoid functions. The global steering model yielded R-squared values ranging from 0.9304 to 0.9934, but for quadratic paths, a model that approximated the width change as linear showed improved goodness-of-fit indices. This is presumably because, according to speed profile and cursor trajectory analyses, participants were unable to effectively utilise the bulging part of the path for acceleration. Our work helps to clarify the behaviours in GUI operations and also offers the possibility of model simplification in applications using the Steering Law, such as difficulty setting in racing video games.

items.title: Validating the Prompt Engineering Expertise Battery (PEEB) as a Combined Self-Report and Performance-Based Measure for Generative AI
items.abstract: Generative AI is used through natural-language prompting, yet few validated measures test whether self-assessed prompting competence matches demonstrated skill. We developed the Prompt Engineering Expertise Battery (PEEB), a 29-item self-report scale and a five-task performance module organized around seven dimensions. In Phase 1 (N = 257), internal consistency was high (α = 0.97), but exploratory parallel analysis retained a single factor, which replicated across random split halves; the scale is therefore scored as one total, captured by a 14-item short form (α = 0.95). In Phase 2, 60 participants completed screen-shared tasks scored by three raters (ICC(2,k) = 0.94). Self-report related only weakly to performance (r = 0.18, 95% CI [−0.07, 0.42]), a preliminary estimate; prompts were brief and disclosed sensitive information in 71% of health tasks. Assessments of prompting competence should include task-based measures, and the structure, short form, and performance module need confirmation in an independent sample.

items.title: What You See Is (Not) What You Got: The Human Factor in PDF Signature Verification
items.abstract: Signed PDF documents have legally binding value under frameworks such as the EU's eIDAS regulation. In this work, we present Genuine PDF Forgeries, a novel attack class that focuses on human factors in signature validation. Our attacks target the disconnect between cryptographically verifiable signer certificates and human-visible signature blocks embedded in documents. We analyze our attacks against 23 PDF viewers and validation tools across desktop platforms and the web. We find that nine of the 13 viewers that automatically report signature validity hide authenticated signer information behind additional user interaction. We then evaluate the attack in twin deception-based online studies with 584 EU-based participants. To further validate the impact, we perform a highly tailored real-world attack study with six trials within two privacy-sensitive organizations. Five of six organizational trials accepted requests authenticated using the forged visual identity. In the online studies (total n=584), the most effective attack variant deceives 71.9% of eligible participants on first impression, and 57.3% continue to be deceived even after we prompt for additional introspection. We derive viewer-side countermeasures and prototype a safeguard that overlays the untrusted signature block with signer information obtained from the validated certificate. Our results show that boolean validity indicators, not associated with the authenticated signer identity, are insufficient in practice.

items.title: When AI Shows Its Rationale: User-Visible Rationale Styles and the Adoption of AI-Mediated Relational Correction
items.abstract: Generative AI is increasingly used to support interpersonal communication, yet little is known about how user-visible rationales shape users’ evaluations of AI-assisted messages. We examine this question in Chinese family group chats, where correcting older relatives’ health misinformation requires factual accuracy alongside care, respect, and face management. In a between-subjects experiment (N = 279), participants viewed the same corrective reply preceded by no visible rationale, a procedural rationale, or a relational rationale. Both rationale conditions increased performance expectancy, effort expectancy, and adoption intention while reducing AI-mediated authenticity concern. Relational rationale produced the largest reduction in authenticity concern, and its effect on performance expectancy strengthened as affective load increased. Overall, user-visible rationales appear to function as communicative frames that shape how users evaluate AI-assisted interpersonal messages, extending research on explainable AI and AI-mediated communication.

items.title: Willingness to Use Personal Health Record Systems: A Mixed-Methods Study Among Multi-Ethnic Civil Servants in an Upper-Middle-Income Country
items.abstract: Abstract Background Electronic personal health record (PHR) systems allow individuals to access and manage their medical records seamlessly across healthcare providers to enhance service delivery and health outcomes. The success of the PHR systems depends on people’s willingness to use (WTU) them. Despite the increasing implementation of this technology in Malaysia, there is a lack of official documentation regarding its acceptance or adoption. Given its high implementation costs, it is essential to gauge the public’s WTU, assess the findings, and take appropriate measures to improve it. Methods This study aimed to determine the WTU as well as understand its predictors and insights among multi-ethnic civil servants from 15 ministries in Putrajaya, Malaysia, using a convergent mixed-methods study. The cross-sectional study was based on the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology with linear regression analysis. Meanwhile, the generic qualitative study was based on semi-structured interviews with thematic analysis. Results The majority of respondents were willing to use the PHR system both currently and in the future. Significant predictors of performance expectancy (PE), facilitating conditions (FC), and social influence (SI) were integrated with the six themes of PE, FC, SI, effort expectancy (EE), human factors (HF), and perceived risk (PR). PE influenced WTU through health status, convenience, administrative efficiency, and incentives, while FC encompassed accessibility, self-efficacy, and assistance. SI depended on the impact of the healthcare provider, social connections, social media figure, promotion, stranger, and sense of autonomy. As for EE, informants underscored the importance of system integration, stability, and user interface. Additionally, HF extended beyond age, gender, and experience to include race, education, income, and employment. Meanwhile, PR was in regard to security, privacy, information credibility, and legal instruments. Conclusion Addressing these domains through tailored strategies can fulfil population needs, enhance system optimization, increase user acceptance, and support sustainable nationwide PHR system adoption.

items.title: 4C/ID Training at UISRAEL
items.abstract: This repository provides materials from a professional development programme at Universidad Tecnológica Israel, Ecuador, on designing instruction around authentic professional tasks using the Four-Component Instructional Design (4C/ID) model. The programme helps university teachers connect syllabus learning outcomes with the integrated knowledge, skills and attitudes required for professional performance. The materials combine explanatory guides, worked design examples, classroom modelling, participant assignments and design worksheets. A continuing example (i.e., conducting a critical literature review to substantiate the preliminary definition of an educational research problem) illustrates how the design decisions connect across sessions. Participants apply the same principles to tasks from their own disciplines. The materials are shared to document the training and support scholarly discussion, reuse and adaptation in higher education. They describe the programme’s instructional rationale and activities; they do not report an empirical evaluation of its effectiveness.

items.title: Acceptance of Training Across Society of Automotive Engineers Levels of Driving Automation
items.abstract: As autonomous vehicles (AVs) become integrated into everyday transportation, developing accurate mental models of automated systems is essential for safe and effective human–vehicle interaction. Inspired by using pre-flight briefings in the aviation industry, this study examined participants’ perceptions of training across the Society of Automotive Engineers (SAE) levels of driving automation. Fifty-one U.S.-based participants were surveyed about their understandings of AV systems, their reliance behaviors on them, and preferences for training across five SAE levels. Our data revealed that most participants preferred receiving some form of training across all levels of automation. Individuals’ personal preferences for mandatory training increased with higher levels of automation and were strongly aligned with their beliefs on legally required training. Additionally, accessible onboarding approaches, particularly in-vehicle tutorials, were identified as the most preferred training format. Overall, our findings highlight the importance of supporting mental model formation to facilitate safe and effective use of AVs.

items.abstract: There is growing recognition of the importance of designing work environments that promote the well-being of diverse employees. Although the Job Demands–Resources (JD–R) model has contributed substantially to work engagement research, there remains scope to extend it to address the challenge of creating inclusive work environments. We examined the associations of workplace tolerance and individual autonomy with work engagement, including the potential mediating roles of psychological safety and intrinsic motivation. We used data from 1084 Japanese workers collected across four waves of online surveys and conducted causal mediation analyses. As a result, the presence of tolerant coworkers was associated with work engagement through workplace psychological safety (total effect = 0.296; proportion mediated = 29.7 %), whereas the absence of intolerant coworkers was not clearly associated with work engagement. Individual autonomy was also associated with work engagement through intrinsic motivation (total effect = 0.444), although the proportion mediated was modest (14.5 %). These findings suggest that positioning workplace tolerance and individual autonomy as social and personal resources, respectively, may extend the JD–R model by enabling it to describe the conditions under which employees with diverse characteristics and circumstances can engage in their work on an equitable basis.

items.title: Association Between Propensity to Trust Automation (PTT) and Personal Characteristics and Traits
items.abstract: This study examined associations between propensity to trust automation (PTT) and 27 other personal characteristic dimensions across 11 constructs: cultural values, attentional control, mood, personality, risk propensity, decision-making style, reasoning, negative attitudes, expectancy, self-efficacy, and the perfect automation schema. A total of 166 participants completed pre-experiment surveys before working with automated drone teammates in a simulated threat-detection task. PTT correlated most strongly with performance expectancy ( r = .46), effort expectancy ( r = .30), negative attitudes toward interacting with autonomous systems ( r = −.28), and the high expectations subscale of the perfect automation schema ( r = .24). Smaller but significant correlations were observed for intellect, masculinity, power distance, and risk propensity. PTT also correlated significantly with post-experiment trust and satisfaction. These results suggest that PTT is associated primarily with expectations about automation and negative attitudes toward interacting with it, and only secondarily with broader personal characteristics.

items.title: Authentication Routines Among College Students
items.abstract: Understanding users’ experiences with authentication is key to developing usable and secure systems, especially in contexts where security risks are high. We conduct a survey and time-diary study ( N = 21) at a large public university to understand the timing and overhead of daily authentication activities across devices and settings. Our findings reveal that people are required to authenticate three times more often than a decade ago (an average of 76 times per day), with an average authentication time overhead of 13.9 min per day. The majority (90.5%) of participants reported frustration with authentication, and 61.9% reported at least one problematic authentication experience that increased their daily temporal and cognitive overhead.

items.title: Between financial, digital, and graph literacy and fraud victimization: Disentangling components and cognitive biases
items.abstract: The rapid digitalisation of financial services has increased individuals’ exposure to online fraud. However, recent literature highlights that identifying a clear profile of fraud victims remains challenging, as individual-level factors examined so far do not fully explain fraud vulnerability. This study examines how financial literacy, digital financial literacy, and financial graph literacy are associated with individuals’ susceptibility to fraud. Moving beyond aggregate measures, the study adopts a multidimensional framework that distinguishes, for both financial and digital financial literacy, between knowledge, attitudes, and behavior, and introduces financial graph literacy as a key capability for interpreting visually presented financial information. The study combines survey-based measures with an embedded experimental task and employs regression and mediation analyses. The findings show that financial and digital financial knowledge are not consistently associated with lower fraud victimization. Higher financial and digital financial attitude scores are associated with lower fraud victimization, whereas higher scores on the financial behavior index are associated with greater reported victimization. Financial graph literacy is also associated with lower fraud victimization. Indirect-effect estimates are consistent with partial mediation through overconfidence for digital financial attitude and financial graph literacy. Financial graph literacy is also associated with lower end-anchoring, i.e. a disproportionate reliance on the final movement of a stock-price graph, but end-anchoring is not associated with fraud victimization. Overall, the study advances a process-oriented and behaviorally grounded understanding of fraud vulnerability, emphasizing the interplay among literacy components and cognitive biases.

items.title: Biased Error Attribution in Multi-Agent Human–AI Systems Under Delayed Feedback
items.abstract: Human decision-making is often influenced by cognitive biases, especially under uncertainty and risk. Prior works have studied biases in single-step decision environments with immediate outcomes or in interaction with a single AI agent. However, less attention has been given to (1) cascaded settings with delayed outcomes, where decision at one step influences future system states and (2) to interaction with multiple AI agents. To study this, we designed a naval battle strategy game where participants interact with two AI advisors. We find asymmetric responses to positive and negative outcomes, with significant changes after negative outcomes. Participants failed to identify the actions responsible for failures and misattributed responsibility across AI agents, leading them to modify decisions steps weakly related to the true cause of poor performance. We refer to this behavior as bias in error attribution. Our findings show how cognitive biases can emerge in human-multi AI teams in cascaded settings.

items.title: Career choice motivations, perceptions, and future intentions among Indian nursing students: a mixed-methods study
items.abstract: Abstract Background: Ensuring a sustainable nursing workforce requires both academic capacity building and a deeper understanding of the experiences that nurture students’ commitment to the profession. In India, rapid growth in nursing education has intersected with changing societal perceptions and competitive career landscapes. This study sought to explore career choice motivations, professional perceptions, and future career intentions among Indian nursing students. Methods: A sequential explanatory mixed-methods approach was gently conducted between April 2025 and June 2026. Phase I involved an online cross-sectional survey (N=1544) across multiple geographical zones. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize the data. Group comparison tests, and multiple linear regression modelling were also used. Phase II comprised semi-structured qualitative interviews (N=27) analyzed using Colaizzi’s descriptive phenomenological approach to better contextualize the statistical findings. Quantitative and qualitative strands were integrated via joint display and narrative synthesis. Results: A notable proportion of participants (69.8%) reported considering alternative career choices, most commonly medicine (37.4%) and technical fields (25.8%). Mean domain scores indicated high intrinsic motivation (19.94 ± 4.61) and economic expectations (20.00 ± 4.11), alongside academic stress (20.03 ± 3.90). Multiple regression analysis (F = 5.085, p < 0.001, R² = 0.103) showed that female gender (B = 4.717, p < 0.001) and salary expectations (B = 1.493, p = 0.002) were positively associated with perception scores, whereas career change intention (B = −4.659, p < 0.001) and higher secondary examination marks (B = −1.905, p = 0.002) were negatively associated. Qualitative findings, organized into seven themes and 27 subthemes, provided explanatory context. Students described how entrance exam setbacks, heavy assignment loads, inconsistent mentorship, and social stigma contributed to uncertainty. In contrast, rewarding patient encounters and the development of clinical confidence fostered a growing sense of professional commitment. Conclusion: Indian nursing students navigate diverse pathways into the profession, balancing altruistic goals with practical challenges and evolving career preferences. The results tentatively highlight that supportive career counseling, refined academic requirements, enhanced clinical mentorship, and clear role definitions may help strengthen students' professional identity and support long-term commitment to nursing practice.

items.title: Children’s Engagement during Cognitive Assessments with Minimal Robot Intervention
items.abstract: Standard pediatric cognitive and projective assessments can be monotonous and provoke anxiety. This reduces children's engagement and compliance and diminishes the quality of observable behavior. In this work, we present a workflow that transfers routine paper-and-pencil tasks to a tablet application and adds a NAO humanoid robot as a social partner. Our goal is to provide a robot-and-tablet system for standardized assessments. In this exploratory study, we focused on quantifying the added contribution of the robot to engagement compared to a tablet-only system. To this end, we evaluated the workflow in a pediatric clinic with 24 participants, each with a distinct neurodevelopmental disorder diagnosis, using a controlled, between-subjects design. The tablet-only condition delivered the same activities and pacing without robot cues. This served as a control to isolate the effect of social scaffolding. Licensed therapists rated engagement using the Pediatric Assessment of Rehabilitation Engagement (PARE) scale. Our preliminary findings suggest that the robot's presence supported higher observable engagement and sustained participation without altering the rapport within the child–therapist–robot triad. Moreover, results in the PARE scale were significantly different between the two conditions when considering the age of the little patients (with mean age 10 vs. 8, respectively). While the small sample size and age distribution warrant cautious interpretation, this work highlights a robot's potential contribution to children's engagement during standardized assessment.

items.title: Cognitive Friction in Human-AI Interactions Across Learning, Work, and Everyday Use: A Scoping Review Protocol
items.abstract: Cognitive friction has been described both as productive resistance intended to sustain cognitive engagement and as effort required to overcome obstacles in AI interaction. These uses create uncertainty about the boundaries of the construct and the mechanisms attributed to it across different contexts. To clarify how cognitive friction is defined and distinguished from related constructs, and to map the mechanisms described as generating it across educational, professional, and everyday human–AI interactions. English-language empirical and non-empirical sources will be eligible where they provide substantive conceptual or mechanistic content relevant to cognitive friction or potentially related constructs in human–AI interaction. Eligible evidence may include journal articles, conference papers, theses, substantive commentaries, and full preprints or working papers. Electronic searches were conducted on 22 October 2026 in Scopus, APA PsycInfo, Web of Science Core Collection, ERIC, arXiv and SSRN. Backward and forward citation searching will supplement these searches. Two reviewers will independently screen records and assess full texts against predefined eligibility criteria. Two reviewers will independently chart data using a structured Google Sheets workbook. Data will be analysed through descriptive mapping and basic qualitative content analysis. items.title: Converged Security Maturity Index: A Unified Model for Cyber, Physical, and Operational Security Maturity Assessment
items.abstract: The growing integration of cyber, physical, and operational security functions has created a need for assessment approaches that evaluate security convergence as an organisational capability rather than as a set of isolated controls. This article proposes the Converged Security Maturity Index (CSMI), a conceptual maturity model designed to assess the level of integration among cybersecurity, physical security, and operational security within organisations. The model is developed using a design science research approach grounded in a structured review of converged security literature, cyber–physical system security, and existing maturity frameworks. CSMI comprises five progressive maturity levels—Fragmented, Coordinated, Integrated, Unified, and Optimised—and evaluates organisational capabilities across four dimensions: governance and strategy, processes and incident management, technology and infrastructure integration, and human factors and organisational culture. The article describes the architecture of the model and the rationale for each maturity level and dimension and outlines how the framework could be applied in practice through a structured questionnaire in future work. The proposed framework aims to support organisational self-assessment, benchmarking, and identification of convergence gaps across different sectors.

items.title: Cybersickness Mitigation in Immersive Virtual Reality Environments: A Systematic Review and Exploratory Meta-Analysis
items.abstract: Cybersickness remains a barrier to immersive virtual reality adoption. This systematic review and exploratory meta-analysis synthesized mitigation studies using head-mounted displays. Six databases were searched for peer-reviewed studies published during 2014–2025 that compared mitigation with a control using standardized sickness outcomes. Risk of bias was assessed using design-appropriate tools. Fifty-nine studies were classified into seven categories; 39 (66%) reported at least one significant reduction. Exploratory random-effects analyses yielded pooled effects for field-of-view restriction (k = 6, g = 0.48) and heterogeneous cognitive/behavioral interventions (k = 3, g = 0.79, I² = 56%). Five of 13 studies using both the Simulator Sickness Questionnaire and Fast Motion Sickness Scale found significant effects only on the latter. No study had low overall risk of bias, and only two reported preregistration. Two provisional frameworks, the Multi-Level Cybersickness Modulation model and Temporal Dynamics Framework, are proposed to generate testable hypotheses and require prospective validation.

items.title: Do Default Effects Shape Cyber Attack Decisions? Lessons From an Empirical Study
items.abstract: Understanding cognitive biases in cyber attacker behavior can help develop countermeasures that leverage predictable mental shortcuts. This paper analyzes the impact of one such bias, the default effect, on cyber attack decisions. Three forms of this effect are examined: explicit default, association effect, and position effect. The experiment included 85 participants who displayed cybersecurity knowledge based on a screening assessment. The participants performed established behavioral tasks and cyber-adapted scenarios involving host selection, port selection, and password spraying. Our findings confirmed that explicit defaults behave as expected from prior research: people preferred the default option more often under opt-out than opt-in framing. For cyber tasks, the association effect was always present and influential as participants preferred options semantically related to the contextual cues provided. In contrast, position effects failed to emerge when semantically meaningful cues were available. Results offer actionable insights for designing cyber defense systems that leverage predictable attacker heuristics.

items.title: Exploring the usage of transparency in supervising uncrewed air traffic management systems
items.abstract: To safely and efficiently manage increasing drone traffic, Uncrewed Air Traffic Management (UTM) is currently being developed with high levels of automation. In low-altitude airspace around airports, human supervision remains essential to ensure safe separation between drones and crewed aircraft, requiring transparency to support oversight of automated decision-making. Although transparency has been shown to improve understanding, trust, and performance, relatively little is known about transparency-seeking behavior during real-time supervision. This article presents a novel on-demand interface for tactical UTM, comprising eight information overlays derived from a consolidated transparency taxonomy that unifies previously fragmented transparency constructs. A human-in-the-loop experiment with 16 participants investigated transparency usage under varying traffic conditions, automation failures, and two autonomous path-planning algorithms: the graph-based Zeta*-SIPP and the sampling-based Informed RRT*. The results show that information about the Closest Point of Approach between drones and crewed aircraft was operationally most valuable. During automation failures, participants increasingly requested information about changes in constraints and traffic situations, together with the planner’s internal reasoning, to diagnose failures and guide intervention decisions. Furthermore, the sampling-based planner revealed an important boundary condition for transparency research: the cognitive costs and benefits of algorithmic transparency during real-time supervision depend on the characteristics of the underlying algorithm and how its search process is presented. Overall, this study shows that transparency requirements are dynamic, depending on user needs, operational context, and the underlying autonomy, and that complementary transparency perspectives can be successfully integrated into a single adaptable interface.

items.title: FRAM-FDM: A Quantitative Safety-II Framework for Runway Overrun Risk Assessment Using Functional Resonance Analysis and Flight Data Monitoring
items.abstract: Abstract Runway overruns rank among the most frequent and economically significant accident categories in commercial aviation, typically arising from the nonlinear combination of performance variabilities during the approach and landing phases. Existing risk models either rely on historical accident databases or treat runway overrun precursors as independent binary events, overlooking the interactive dynamics of everyday flight operations. This paper introduces FRAM-FDM, a quantitative methodology that integrates the Functional Resonance Analysis Method (FRAM) with Flight Data Monitoring (FDM) to assess and manage operational runway overrun risk from a Safety-II perspective. The methodology deconstructs the approach-and-landing sociotechnical system into functional couplings, quantifies their output variabilities using real flight data recorder (FDR) data, and aggregates them through: (i) linear regression combined with Monte Carlo Simulation (MCS) for probabilistic fleet-level risk estimation; (ii) logistic regression with odds-ratio analysis to rank precursor influence; and (iii) metadata-driven scenario simulation in the FRAM Model Visualiser (FMV). Applied to a case study of 110 landings — including one overrun event — from a business jet fleet, the framework identifies airspeed excess at the runway threshold and brake application profile as the dominant risk contributors, demonstrates synergistic risk amplification when multiple variabilities co-occur, and provides actionable guidance for training and procedure reinforcement. FRAM-FDM advances FRAM toward a fully quantitative, data-driven implementation and aligns FDM programmes with Safety-II principles.

items.title: Frequency and purpose of artificial intelligence tool use and their associations with academic motivation and self-efficacy among medical students: a cross-sectional study
items.abstract: Abstract Background Artificial intelligence (AI) tools are increasingly used by medical students for academic purposes, yet how patterns of such use relate to academic motivation and self-efficacy remain insufficiently characterized, particularly in the Iranian medical education context. This study examined the frequency and purpose of AI tool use among medical students and their associations with academic motivation and academic self-efficacy. Methods A descriptive-analytical cross-sectional study was conducted among medical students at Kashan University of Medical Sciences, Iran, in 2026. Using proportionate stratified sampling across four educational stages, 111 students completed a questionnaire package comprising a researcher-developed AI-use instrument (separate frequency and purpose scores), the Persian Academic Motivation Scale, and the Persian College Academic Self-Efficacy Scale. Associations between the two AI-use scores and five outcomes (self-efficacy, intrinsic motivation, extrinsic motivation, amotivation, and composite positive motivation) were examined using Spearman correlation with Bonferroni correction, followed by five multiple linear regression models adjusting for age, sex, educational stage, and GPA. Results Conversational AI tools, most notably ChatGPT, were used by nearly all participants. Both AI-use frequency and purpose were positively correlated with academic self-efficacy, intrinsic motivation, extrinsic motivation, and positive motivation, and negatively correlated with amotivation (Spearman ρ = 0.46–0.77; all p < 0.001, surviving Bonferroni correction). In adjusted models, AI-use purpose remained independently associated with all five outcomes (standardized β = 0.32–0.69), whereas AI-use frequency remained independently associated only with self-efficacy (β = 0.55, p < 0.001). GPA was independently associated with intrinsic motivation, extrinsic motivation, and positive motivation, but not self-efficacy or amotivation. No significant differences by sex or educational stage were observed. The five models explained 40% to 61% of outcome variance. Conclusions The purpose for which medical students use AI tools showed more consistent independent associations with academic motivation and self-efficacy than frequency of use alone, suggesting that how AI is used may be more relevant to these outcomes than how often it is used. As an observational, cross-sectional study, these findings describe association rather than causal sequence, and contribute context-specific evidence on AI use and its psychological correlates among medical students in Iran.

items.title: Growth Paths in Early Machine Learning Ventures: Technical Configuration and Competitive Advantage Over Time
items.abstract: Machine learning capabilities have become important strategic assets, yet little is known about how their technical characteristics affect the competitive advantage of the firms that build them. Through an inductive, multicase study tracking six early-stage machine learning ventures in an accelerator program, we explore how their phases of specialization and exploration may be constrained by properties of the underlying technology. Our findings show how training data, learning paradigms, and model outputs depend on one another and on the applications they serve, and how these relationships change over time. This interdependence shapes firms’ growth paths, alternately expanding or limiting the strategic options available to them. Characteristics that confer an early competitive advantage can constrain later growth. We discuss the implications for strategy research on competitive advantage and path dependence in machine learning ventures.

items.title: How much can a human being lift? A Bayesian latent capability model for Olympic weightlifting
items.abstract: Estimates of the limits of human performance are usually built on record books, on the premise that a record is the best an athlete could do. In Olympic weightlifting the premise fails, because the competitor declares the weight before each of three attempts per lift and only the heaviest successful attempt is recorded, so a record is a lower bound, chosen by the athlete, on a maximal capability never observed. We treat the maximal lift of each competitor on each competition day as a latent variable, of which every attempt is a trial and every declared weight a measurement. Its distribution at a given bodyweight follows an extreme value mixture model with an estimated threshold, and an athlete-specific random effect links the competitions of each athlete. The model is fitted to the 117,892 attempts of 5,040 athletes in 141 international competitions between 2017 and 2026. The upper tail of capability is bounded, with posterior probability above 0.999 for men, 0.96 for the women's snatch and 0.94 for the women's clean and jerk. At 110 kilograms of bodyweight the men's ceiling lies one to three per cent above the heaviest lifts, against twelve and sixteen per cent for women at 86 kilograms. The record book alone places the men's ceiling six and twelve kilograms higher, because the best lift of a day ending on a success overstates capability.

items.title: Minimally Invasive Surgery and Emerging Technologies in Emergency Abdominal Surgery: A Narrative Review Focusing on Indocyanine Green Fluorescence, Robotic Assistance and Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Minimally invasive surgery (MIS) is progressively transforming emergency abdominal care through high-definition visualization, indocyanine green (ICG) fluorescence imaging, robotic-assisted platforms and the emerging integration of artificial intelligence (AI). This narrative review traces the evolution from conventional laparoscopy to fluorescence-guided, robotic-assisted and AI-supported emergency surgery. Publications were identified in PubMed, EMBASE, and Web of Science, prioritizing guidelines, consensus statements, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and recent clinical studies. Current evidence supports a laparoscopic-first approach in hemodynamically stable patients with acute appendicitis, acute calculous cholecystitis, perforated peptic ulcer and selected cases of adhesive small bowel obstruction, strangulated hernia, complicated diverticulitis and penetrating trauma, whereas open laparotomy remains mandatory in hemorrhagic or septic shock. Near-infrared ICG imaging has expanded from elective to emergency practice for biliary anatomy identification, bowel perfusion assessment and anastomotic decision-making, although prospective emergency data remain limited. Robotic systems offer dexterity, ergonomics and integrated imaging, but emergency use is constrained by availability, cost, docking time and team training. AI is being explored for anatomy recognition, risk prediction, augmented reality and autonomous subtasks, with decision support the most realistic near-term role. The value of these technologies depends less on the technology itself than on patient selection, surgical expertise, team preparedness and institutional readiness.

items.title: Online, offline, and hybrid identity: Exploring domain-based social identities and their implications for technology attitudes, wellbeing, and social cohesion
items.abstract: Online identity typically has been conceptualized either in terms of online social roles or in terms of identification with specific online groups. In this paper we explore whether people can form a meaningful identity from the online domain itself , seeing themselves collectively as ‘online people’, ‘offline people’, or in terms of a hybrid online/offline self-categorization. Results from a survey study of 200 participants supported this idea, such that the means of online, offline, or hybrid person variables were significantly above the midpoint of the scale and the majority of participants identified most strongly in terms of one of these identities. Factor analysis, correlations, variable network analysis, and textual analysis suggested that online and offline social identity are orthogonal constructs. Moreover, online identity was related to, but distinct from, hybrid identity (being a person who lives both online and offline). Supporting predictions derived from social digital identity theory (SDIT), each kind of domain-based identification uniquely predicted higher trust in the relevant ingroup only. Moreover, in line with predictions, online identification uniquely predicted more positive attitudes towards technology. However, contrary to predictions, the different kinds of domain-based social identification did not uniquely predict wellbeing or social cohesion. Hybrid and offline identification also failed to uniquely predict technology attitudes. Furthermore, when controlling for hybrid identification, being more ‘online’ in terms of online technology use did not significantly predict wellbeing or social cohesion outcomes. These findings represent an initial exploration of ‘domain-based’ social identities and their implications.

items.title: Rational Use of Time for Social Coordination in Humans and AI
items.abstract: All social interactions are situated in time. Previous studies have shown that humans are able to use implicit temporal cues, such as the duration of a pause, to infer others' mental states. But how do humans use temporal cues for dynamic, fine-grained social coordination? And can AI systems do the same, without ``experiencing'' continuous real-time as humans do? We study these questions using a cooperative card game task called The Mind, which requires players to achieve a shared goal across repeated interactions but forbids explicit communication: the only available signal is the passage of time. We evaluate 150 humans, and two classes of AI models which reflect different ways of operationalizing time in artificial systems: computer-use agents (CUAs), and standard text-prompted LLMs. We find that human behavior is best captured by a Bayesian strategy that infers a partner's belief from their timing---and similarly for frontier models. However, unlike humans, none of the tested models seem to efficiently adapt their behaviors to their partners' over the course of the game. From a cognitive perspective, our findings suggest that humans perform implicit probabilistic reasoning about continuous-time signals in dynamic social settings, and that such reasoning mechanisms may emerge without real-time experience. Practically, our study highlights new challenges for AI systems to coordinate efficiently with other agents by learning to interpret and adapt to their implicit signals in dynamic settings.

items.title: Repertoires of Contention: Building computational tools and infrastructures for community resistance to bitcoin mining
items.abstract: Recent work in human-computer interaction and allied fields has sought to engage community members as co-designers, facilitators, and decision makers to challenge structural power barriers and knowledge gaps. In this paper, we apply a diverse set of computational techniques to engage and address community concerns surrounding the socio-environmental impacts of the Greenidge Bitcoin mining power plant facility in upstate New York. Through collaborative interactions with community groups, addressing problems ranging from regulatory inertia to thermal water pollution, we aim to facilitate not just the production of new and critical environmental knowledge but also new computationally-supported repertoires of contention: means of contesting the unequal relations of knowledge and power that structure and often determine the outcomes of environmental controversies. We argue such engagements can help support more politically engaged forms of HCI, oriented towards efforts to redress and repair disparities in wealth, knowledge, and influence through strategic sociotechnical interventions and alliances.

items.title: The Effects of Automated Vehicle Behavior Explanations on Drivers’ Physiological Responses in High-Risk Situations
items.abstract: Automated vehicles (AVs) have the potential to improve road safety, but unexpected behaviors in safety-critical situations can increase driver discomfort, stress, and distrust. While prior work suggests that AV explanations may improve trust, anxiety, and user experience, their physiological effects remain underexplored. This pilot study examined whether speech-based explanations influence driver stress after safety-critical driving events. Fourteen participants viewed five 2-min driver-perspective driving videos that varied by risk level and explanation condition. Heart rate and galvanic skin response were analyzed during the 40 s following each explanation. Results showed that explanations were associated with significantly higher LF/HF ratios in both low risk and high risk conditions, higher GSR mean amplitude in low-risk conditions, and higher SDNN in high-risk conditions. Explanations increased physiological arousal, potentially indicating greater engagement and attention. Findings may inform intelligent AV explanation systems that support safer real-time driver feedback.

items.title: To Bot or not To Bot: Integrating a Social Robot into the Actor’s Rehearsal Process
items.abstract: Effective theatrical rehearsal is essential for actors’ character development, involving intricate cognitive, emotional, and physical processes. Despite well-established traditional techniques that combine individual practice and partner interactions, rehearsal often requires significant time and resources. Emerging digital and robotic technologies present novel opportunities to enhance rehearsal methods; however, their potential as interactive rehearsal aids remains largely unexplored. This research examines the role of a social robot in supporting actors during pre-rehearsal or solo preparation of two scenes from Tennessee Williams’ The Glass Menagerie (1944). Thirty actors with different levels of experience participated in three rehearsal settings: solo practice, rehearsal with a robot playing one character, and rehearsal with the robot alternating between two roles. We evaluated the robot's impact via qualitative responses and self-reports. Thematic analysis indicated that robot-assisted rehearsal improved participants’ experience compared to solo rehearsal, especially among less experienced actors. The robot's role-switching capability offered additional depth appreciated mainly by seasoned performers. These outcomes highlight the promise of social robots as rehearsal tools adapted to the experience of actors.

items.title: Understanding organisations’ responsibilities and readiness for occupational road safety: Implications for saving lives beyond 2025
items.abstract: Most organisations generate travel and transport and thus influence traffic safety. Nevertheless, their roles and responsibilities for occupational road safety remain poorly understood. This study examines organisational readiness for occupational road safety with a particular focus on the relationship between organisations’ perceptions of traffic safety and the implementation of traffic safety measures. The study is based on a survey of organisational representatives in 109 companies in Sweden in 2025. The survey consists of two questionnaires capturing organisational commitment and reported measures to improve traffic safety in organisations’ roles as employers and transport buyers. An employer questionnaire focuses on traffic safety requirements for employees’ work-related travel and organisational vehicle fleets, while a transport procurement questionnaire captures the requirements on transport procurement. Organisational readiness for occupational road safety is analysed using Organisational Readiness for Implementing Change (ORIC), including perceived capacity to influence traffic safety, views on responsibility, and the integration of traffic safety into occupational health and safety (OHS) or sustainability practices. The results show that many organisations have policies for work-related travel and set traffic safety requirements for their vehicles, while such requirements in transport procurement remain limited. Regression analyses indicate that organisations with higher readiness are more likely to set traffic safety requirements, particularly regarding work-related travel. The findings highlight the need to strengthen organisations’ awareness of their roles and responsibilities, clarify expectations for organisations from authorities, and further integrate traffic safety into organisational management systems to reduce road traffic fatalities and injuries, in line with the global road safety agenda, often framed as “saving lives beyond 2025”.

items.title: What makes human contribution recognisable in AI-mediated work? Attributional labour and gendered recognition in apprenticeships in England
items.abstract: Abstract Debates around generative artificial intelligence frequently organise workplace change through automation and augmentation, leaving less visible the organisational work through which human contribution remains interpretable once production is shared with generative systems. Drawing on semi-structured interviews with 18 women in business-related apprenticeships in England, analysed through reflexive thematic analysis and abductive engagement with sociotechnical AI research, labour-process scholarship and feminist accounts of recognition, the study develops a mechanism-oriented account in which organisational rules delimit legitimate AI use, selected execution tasks accelerate, and verification, contextual judgement and accountable decision-making remain attached to apprentices. Where AI-mediated production made polished output a weaker standalone indicator of individual capability, some participants described supplementing performance with additional evidentiary work that rendered contribution, judgement and responsibility more legible to evaluators. This evaluator-facing work is conceptualised as attributional labour, a reconfiguration of pre-existing recognition demands whose form changes when technologically mediated artefacts reveal less about the human competence behind them. The organisational costs and returns associated with this work appeared to vary with occupational hierarchy, managerial proximity and the valuation of administrative and relational work. Augmentation consequently emerges as an organisational recognition settlement in which technical capacity, hidden human work and evaluative authority are redistributed together.

items.title: AI Is Not an Employee: Workplace Mental Models and the Context Discovery Gap in Human-AI Interaction
items.abstract: AI adoption can falter not because systems lack capability, but because organizations apply employee mental models to systems that do not participate in work as socially embedded employees. This article develops a theoretical model of that mismatch, drawing on theory of mind, psychological contracts, shared mental models, transactive memory, and automation reliance research. It introduces the context discovery gap: a mismatch between the organizational context people assume AI already has or will discover and the context it can actually obtain and use in a workplace. Employee-associated expectations may contribute to this mismatch by leading users to leave relevant background unstated. The article argues that the missing psychology of AI adoption lies in the human assumptions through which AI systems are understood, delegated to, and evaluated. As a conceptual contribution, it connects these assumptions to context provision and reliance, develops testable propositions, and identifies responsibilities for designing and maintaining context discovery.

items.title: Building World Models from Intrinsic Motivation
items.abstract: In the absence of extrinsic rewards or task supervision, human behavior is guided by intrinsic motivation---neural signals that drive curiosity, creativity, play, and other essential facets of intelligence. Intrinsic motivation plays an important developmental role in building robust world models that enable generalization and adaptation. Yet existing studies leave open how a broad range of intrinsic motivations interacts with world-model representation learning to support downstream control. This limits our understanding of which intrinsically collected experiences build reusable models. To address these gaps, we integrate 24 intrinsic objectives, including established methods and explicit variants spanning curiosity, entropy, and competency, into a common model-based reinforcement learning framework. We evaluate the world models they build through zero-shot, few-shot, and multi-task control in locomotion, manipulation, and open-ended gaming environments, using three representation-learning strategies: observation reconstruction, latent prediction, and redundancy reduction. Curiosity-driven exploration with observation reconstruction yields the strongest aggregate family profile, although the best individual pairing depends on the experiment. In compositional vision-based tasks, intrinsic motivation derived from both episodic and lifelong novelty---providing a complementary memory to the world model's generic recurrent state---achieves the best zero-shot transfer and few-shot adaptation. These findings motivate designing intrinsic motivation and representation learning jointly. Our results demonstrate world models as a powerful tool for measuring the quality of intrinsically motivated experience, and positions intrinsic motivation as a key ingredient for building world models autonomously.
